en: The Jayamaṅgalā: A Commentary on the Seventy Verses of Sāṃkhya.
Having prostrated before the Sage who teaches the supramundane, who has attained the light of reality;
The commentary on the *Saptatikā*, titled *Jayamaṅgalā*, is composed.

Since wise people do not engage in any activity when the purpose has not been stated, the purpose is declared: liberation results from the knowledge of reality; the principles (tattvas) are twenty-five.
And so it has been said:
"One who knows the twenty-five principles, regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) they delight in,"
Whether one has matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter. Thus it is said.
And regarding the phrase "in those [treatises] renowned as the *Ṣaṣṭitantra* and so forth":
because the *Ṣaṣṭitantra* is extensive, the *Saptatikā* was composed for the sake of favoring sentient beings who take pleasure in concise works.
And he will say: "This has been summarized by the Noble Ones."
If it is asked what the fruit of liberation is, it is the cessation of suffering.
One who does not know reality remains transmigrating, struck by sufferings;
but through the knowledge of reality, one attains absolute isolation (kaivalya).
One is not struck down by sufferings. Regarding the question "What is the reason that should be investigated when one is being struck? he says here:
"Because of the assault of the threefold suffering, there is an inquiry into the means for its removal."
If it is argued that [the means of knowledge] are useless with respect to what is already seen, we say no, because there is an absence [of such objects] neither absolutely nor ultimately.
"From the affliction by the threefold suffering, there arises the desire to know," and so forth.
The "threefold suffering" (*duḥkhatraya*) refers to the triad of sufferings: internal (*ādhyātmika*), [external (*ādhibhautika*), and celestial (*ādhidaivika*)].
Namely, that which pertains to living beings (ādhibhautika) and that which pertains to divine forces (ādhidaivika). That which is within the self is the internal (adhyātma).
In that regard, that which occurs is internal;
it is both physical and mental.
Among these, suffering such as fever arises from the imbalance of wind, bile, and phlegm.
That which exists in the body is called *śārīra* (bodily). That suffering which arises in the mind through desire, anger, grief, and so forth, is *mānasa* (mental).
That which occurs with reference to humans, domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and stationary beings is *ādhibhautika* (pertaining to other beings).
That which occurs with reference to divine factors, such as possession by malevolent spirits (*graha*) and the like, within the body is called *ādhidaivika*.
These constitute the threefold suffering.
From the cause of being struck or afflicted by these, there arises *jijñāsā*—the desire to know.
To the question "In what object? he says: "In the cause that destroys it.
It is called "destroying" (avaghātaka) because it strikes down (avaghātayati) or removes (apanayati).
That which destroys the threefold suffering is "that-destroyer" (tadavaghātaka).
There is a prohibition of the sixth-case compound with words ending in *tṛc* and *aka*;
thus, [the rule] "that which instigates it is the cause (*hetu*)" does not apply.
Indeed, one desires to know the cause that brings about these sufferings, thinking, "By what means do these sufferings arise?
It is a common saying: "I am a sufferer; I seek a remedy for this.
And it is held in the mind that this [remedy] is none other than the knowledge of the twenty-five principles (*tattva*).
"If it is argued that [the practice] is useless regarding what is seen":
this might be so if there were no visible cause for its destruction;
however, as long as there exists a remedy prescribed by the science of medicine (*cikitsā-śāstra*) for the removal of internal physical suffering, [the objection does not hold].
The power of mental calculation, as well as the objects of the senses such as sound and so forth—
whether pertaining to the physical world (ādhibhautika) or the divine realm (ādhidaivika)— are seen in this very world to be practiced as causes of affliction.
Because these two are counter-balanced by their respective opposites:
therein, for the celestial [obstacles], there are undertakings consisting of the means of conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force;
and for the elemental [obstacles] as well, there are [remedies] such as taking refuge in sheltered places, avoiding falls and collisions, and so forth.

Furthermore, suspecting that the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) regarding this subject would be useless once the cause has been perceived, he says: "Because of the absence [of the cause] in an absolute and ultimate sense.
It is not purposeless; it is indeed purposeful.
Why? Because of its absence in an absolute sense—that is, because of its absence in both an absolute and an ultimate sense.
The meaning is that there is no absolute and ultimate absence of suffering.
For even when the observed means are employed, the threefold suffering certainly occurs for some; thus, there is no absolute cessation.
Furthermore, because it arises again after some sort of cessation, there is no ultimate cessation.
Therefore, it is appropriate to have the desire to know [the means] for the sake of the absolute and final cessation of suffering.
// 1 // If this is so, there exists a cause for the absolute and final cessation of suffering prescribed by the Veda. And thus it has been said:
"We have drunk Soma; we have become immortal; we have reached the light; we have found the gods.
What can hostility do to us? And what can the malice of a mortal do to the immortal? Thus [it is said].
The meaning of this is as follows: Indra said to the gods who were unlearned, "O divine ones, is there any other happiness? They said to him, "There is none;
we have drunk the Soma."
Having drunk the Soma, we have become immortal;
we have become those from whom death has departed.
"We have gone to the light.
This "light" is heaven;
we have reached it.
"We have found the gods," they said;
this means they knew, "This many gods are in this heaven," that is, knowledge has arisen within us. "What could it do to us? they asked.
It is said that death acts [against us];
what will death do to us who drink Soma? Even ill-will—that is, disease—[will not affect us].
"Even that terrible old age— what will it do to us,
who are immortal?
Thus, in this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) that there exists a cause for the cessation of suffering through the drinking of soma—
The revealed (ānuśravika) [means] is like the perceived (dṛṣṭa), for it is characterized by impurity, perishability, and excess;
superior to that is the [knowledge] which is its opposite, arising from the discernment of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower.
"Like the seen, [is] the revealed (ānuśravika)," and so forth.
It is called *anuśrava* because it is heard (*anuśrūyate*) through tradition; *anuśrava* refers to the Veda, according to the rule *śruvaḥ ṛdor ap*.
That which originates therein as a cause is *ānuśravika*.
"Internal and so forth";
"like what is seen" means similar to what is perceived,
because one perceives defects in that as well.

As it has been said: "For that [means] is associated with impurity, destruction, and excess. Because the scriptural means (ānuśravika-hetu) is associated with these three defects, beginning with impurity;
therein, in the case of the Agnihotra and other rites, it is associated with impurity due to the slaughter of animals and the drinking of soma.
Because of the exhaustion of karma there is a fall from heaven; thus, it is characterized by decay.
As they have said: "Many thousands of Indras have passed away in age after age";
and, "For even among the gods, he is a god who grows poor."
"Upon seeing the Lord, great suffering arises";
this is [an example of] being possessed of excellence.
For instance, he who performs a hundred sacrifices possesses great sovereignty.
For one who [attains results] by means of two or three [factors], that is "slight.
Therefore, even that which is based on tradition (ānuśravika) should be abandoned, just like [views] based on direct perception (dṛṣṭa).
Then, asking "Which one is superior?", he says: "The opposite of that is superior.
That which is the opposite of the empirical and the scriptural—namely, what is called the knowledge of reality—is superior, because it brings about absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
In that regard, it is superior to what is seen because of its absolute and ultimate non-existence;
for by the abandonment of the body, it has pure fruit,
and by the abandonment of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), it has inexhaustible fruit.
And because it is unsurpassed, its fruit is without superior; thus, it is superior to that which is heard from tradition.
To the question "How is that stated?", he says: "Through the discernment of the Manifest, the Unmanifest, and the Knower.
By means of these three groups, the twenty-five principles (tattvas) are described.
Among them, that which consists of twenty-three types, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the gross elements (bhūta), is called the Manifest (vyakta).
Because the Pradhāna is manifested through that form;
the Pradhāna is unmanifest because it is unmanifest in some other form.
One who knows is a "knower" (jña), namely the person (puruṣa).
The meaning is that [the fruit] is obtained from that discernment (vijñāna) which is the determination of their own nature within those [objects].

For, having distinguished [the self] from the body and so forth, through the practice thereof, the knowledge of the distinction between primordial matter (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa) arises at a later time;
and from that, isolation (kaivalya) follows.
Of this Āryā verse, those [verses] which are to be spoken next—

Root-nature is unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both nature and evolutes;
the group of sixteen is the evolute;
and the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor evolute. (ISk 3)
‘Root-nature’ (*mūlaprakṛti*), and so forth.
*Prakṛti* means *pradhāna* (the primary cause). It is called *prakṛti* because from it everything is produced (*prakriyate*) or originates.
It is called *mūlaprakṛti* because it is both the root (*mūla*) and the primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The meaning is that it is the root—the primary cause—of the seven natures.
"Non-modification" (*avikṛti*): it is called non-modification because it is not modified; the meaning is that it is not produced from anything whatsoever.
This is the first reality.

"Seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both evolvents and evolutes. Here, "the Great One" refers to the intellect (buddhi); those primordial natures (prakṛtis) of which it is the first are so described.
They are called "evolvents and evolutes" because they are both primordial natures and transformations.
In this context, *prakṛti* (nature) is that which generates the great *ahaṅkāra* (ego), while being itself a *vikṛti* (modification) produced from the Great Principle (*mahat*).
The five subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*)— sound, touch, form, taste, and smell— are *prakṛtis* when they generate the gross elements known respectively as ether, air, fire, water, and earth.
The transformations arising from the ego-principle—
these are the seven principles.
"And the group of sixteen is the transformation.
That which has sixteen as its measure is "the sixteenfold" (ṣoḍaśaka). [It consists of] the five sense organs of cognition (buddhīndriya),...
The five organs of action,
the mind, and thus eleven organs, together with the five great elements— this is the group of sixteen.
The particle *ca* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*.
"Modification" (*vikāra*) means "transformation" (*vikṛti*) alone;
the meaning is that nothing whatsoever is produced from this.
These are the sixteen principles (*tattva*).
"The *puruṣa* is neither nature (*prakṛti*) nor a transformation (*vikṛti*).
It is called *puruṣa* because it dwells within the *pura*, which is the body.
The method here is etymological:
therefore, nothing whatsoever is produced, and thus there is no primordial nature (*prakṛti*),
because it is devoid of activity.
Nor does this arise from anything else, and thus it is not a modification (*vikṛti*), because it is beginningless.
Regarding the proof of these [categories], such as the manifest (*vyakta*) and so forth, he states the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): [Kārikā 4]
Perception, inference,
and authoritative testimony are accepted as the threefold means of valid cognition, because all means of valid cognition are established within these.
For the establishment of the objects of cognition proceeds from the means of valid cognition.
‘Seen’ (dṛṣṭam), and so forth.
‘Seen’ means direct perception (pratyakṣa). That by which something is inferred is inference (anumāna).

An authoritative person (āpta) is one whose defects have been eliminated; that which is spoken by him is authoritative speech (āptavacana), which is scripture (āgama). These three are accepted as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
But surely there are other means of valid cognition as well, such as intuition and so forth; for it has been said:
"Intuition, analogy, tradition, non-existence, possibility, and likewise presumptive implication—others have declared these to be the means of valid cognition."
Regarding this prima facie argument, it says: "Because it is established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This means that because all means of valid cognition, such as intuition (*pratibhā*) and so forth, are established, [intuition] is included within these three types [of valid cognition].
In that regard, the notion that "it exists in that village or city" is a conceptual construction (*pratibhā*) that has arisen;
however, when one whose faults have been exhausted attains supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), it becomes direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Because its defects are not exhausted, that [cognition] is invalid due to its falsity.

Even that which is occasionally non-contradictory with respect to its object is merely inference (*anumāna*), since it arises from a specific occasional cause, and is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"The gavaya is like a cow": this is comparison (*aupamya*).
In that regard, someone who does not know a gavaya asks a reliable person, "What is a gavaya like?"
He said to him, "As is a cow, so is a gavaya.

This is merely the word of a reliable authority (āptavacana) and not a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Even when, having received this instruction, he sees a gavaya, [it is still based on that prior testimony].

Even then, since one initiates the linguistic usage of a *gavaya* by means of the very mark (*liṅga*) such as its horns which was seen in a cow, this is nothing but inference (*anumāna*) and not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"Thus indeed Vaiśravaṇa [did]"—
this is tradition (*aitihya*).
This is merely the word of a reliable authority (*āptavacana*) and not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
The collection of particles *iti ha* occurs in the sense of a traditional instruction (*upadeśapāramparya*);
thus, *itiha* itself is *aitihya*.
The suffix *yañ* is used in the sense of the base itself;
thus, "there is no jar here because of non-perception" constitutes non-existence (*abhāva*).
In that regard, the absence of a jar is simply the location devoid of a jar;
and since that is established by the means of valid cognition known as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is not a separate means of valid cognition.
It is also possible [to say] that when it is stated, "A *prastha* of mung beans," this implies "four *kuḍavas*."

Such is this "origination" (sambhava). In that case, because there is a determination of the whole (samudāya) through its parts (avayava), which possess the mark (liṅgin), it is indeed inference (anumāna). Since the whole is produced by its parts, the relationship is characterized as that between cause and effect (kāryakāraṇa).
"When it is stated that 'Devadatta does not eat during the day and is strong,' it follows by implication that he eats at night"; this is presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Therefore, the cognition of him [eating] at night is not distinct from inference (*anumāna*).
And this very [reason] is called "the impossibility otherwise" (anyathānupapatti).
If it is asked, "What is the purpose of defining the three means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? he says:

"For the establishment of the object of cognition (prameya) is from the means of valid cognition. Since the establishment of the object to be known occurs through the means of valid cognition, otherwise how could there be its attainment or avoidance? // 4 //
Karika 5: He states the definition of perception and the other means of valid cognition:
"Perception is the ascertainment of each respective object."
Inference has been declared to be threefold:
that which is preceded by the mark (liṅga) and the possessor of the mark (liṅgin), as well as authoritative scripture, which is the word of a reliable person (āptavacana). ISk_5 //
"Apprehension with respect to each respective object," and so forth.
"Prati-viṣayam" means toward each individual object; apprehension with respect to each respective object is "prativiṣayādhyavasāyaḥ."
The objects are sound and the rest;
ascertainment is the intellect (*buddhi*).

That intellect which arises—predominantly characterized by the determination of specific qualities—through the doors of the auditory, tactile, visual, gustatory, and olfactory organs with respect to sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, is "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*).
Because it is pure, it is a valid means of knowledge; because it is impure, it is not a valid means of knowledge. That [means of knowledge] is fourfold: with designation, conceptual, and so forth.
It is both distinct from the object and distinct from the sense faculty.
In that regard, when one sees someone approaching from a distance and perceives a resemblance to Devadatta, the cognition that arises—namely, "This is Devadatta"—is conceptual;
because it is characterized by doubt, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
The vision of two moons by one suffering from ophthalmia is distinct from that object, because there is no second moon;
likewise, that which is seen in a dream is distinct from the sense faculties.
Because the sense faculties are overwhelmed by sleep.
"Threefold inference has been declared"; thus it is explained in the *Ṣaṣṭitantra*: "pūrvavat," "śeṣavat," [and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa].
Regarding "inference based on general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*):
there are three categories of objects—past, future, and present.
Among these, inference "like the former" (*pūrvavat*) is for the purpose of establishing a future object.
"Pūrvavat" (the prior-like) is so called because it possesses a prior mark (*liṅga*);

for example, having seen a rising cloud, one infers that rain will occur. "Śeṣavat" (the remainder-like) is for the purpose of establishing a past object; it is so called because it possesses a remaining mark (*liṅga*).
For example, when it has rained upon this river,
the remaining turbid water is the *liṅga* (the mark).

For the purpose of establishing a present object, there is the *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [type of inference], because the relationship between the *liṅga* and the *liṅgin* (the possessor of the mark) has been observed through a general rule.
Just as Devadatta’s arrival at another location is observed to be preceded by motion,
so too is the motion of the sun and other celestial bodies inferred from their general arrival at another location.
"It is preceded by the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin). Thus, inference is of three kinds;
it is observed in the world to be sometimes preceded by the mark and sometimes preceded by the bearer of the mark.

For example, a cuckoo is sometimes inferred by its audible cry; and sometimes, having seen the cuckoo as the possessor of the mark (liṅgin), one concludes that it must also possess its audible cry. Thus, these two stand in the relationship of the signified and the signifier when a connection exists.

And there are seven types of connections: among them, the relationship of owner and owned is, for instance, between a king and his servant, where sometimes the king is known through the servant, or the servant through the king.
Thus, the relationship between the primary material and its modification is like that of barley and flour;
the relationship between cause and effect is like that of a cow and its calf;
and the relationship between a container and its contents is like that of a bowl and the rice within it.
The relationship of association is, for example, like that between two ruddy geese (*cakravāka*).
The relationship of opposition is, for example, like that between cold and heat;
in that case, the absence of one is perceived when the other is present.
The relationship between the sign and the signified is like that between the food and the eater;
by means of these relationships, the threefold inference as a valid means of knowledge is not lost.
"Reliable scripture and the word of a reliable person. Here, a "reliable person" (āpta) is one whose defects have been exhausted. As they say:
"One who is devoted to his own duty and is free from passion and hatred [is a reliable person]."
Free from enmity and honored by the virtuous—he who is such should be known as a trustworthy person. Thus it is said.
The word of an authoritative person (*āptavacana*) is that scripture which has come down through a lineage of oral tradition from authorities;
it is an object perceived or inferred by them,
which is taught by means of words for the sake of producing in another a cognition similar to their own cognition.
That which is another’s word does not float [in uncertainty].

The word "and" (ca) is intended to demonstrate that it stands on an equal footing with inference (*anumāna*). Just as authoritative cognition has the three times as its object, so too does the word of a reliable person (*āptavacana*). // 5 //
Regarding these three, which one has which object? To this he says:
"But from what is perceived in a general way, there is the cognition of supersensible things through inference."
Therefore, even that which is unestablished and beyond the senses is established through authoritative scripture (āptāgama).
"Generally speaking," and so forth.
The objects of cognition (*prameya*) are threefold: the perceptible (*pratyakṣa*), the imperceptible (*parokṣa*), and [the remote (*parokṣatara*)].
And [there is] that which is absolutely beyond perception (*atyantaparokṣa*).
In this regard, from that inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭam anumānam*), there is the establishment of things that are beyond the senses and imperceptible;
that is their ascertainment (*niścaya*).
This is because those [objects] are within the range of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

As for the two types of inference—*pūrvavat* (based on what precedes) and *śe�ṣavat* (based on what remains)—since they operate upon future and past objects respectively, it is impossible for them to function regarding present objects that are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).
"Therefore, even from this, it is unestablished"; thus,

that which is unestablished and beyond perception through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is established through scripture (*āgama*), because it is absolutely beyond perception.
Just as in the case of heaven and liberation;
however, regarding the object of cognition that is perceptible, it is stated by implication that only what is actually perceived is operative. // 6 // Kārikā 7:
Now, one might object: "From the discernment of the Manifest, the Unmanifest, and the Knower.

While the Manifest is indeed established through perception and inference, how can there be an establishment of the Pradhāna and Puruṣa, since they are never perceived? To this we reply: non-existence does not follow from mere non-perception.
Since the perception of even existing objects occurs through four modes—
due to defects of place, defects of the sense faculties, defects of the object, and defects of other factors—
he says the following, showing them specifically:
Due to excessive distance, extreme proximity, impairment of the sense organs, instability of the mind, subtlety, obstruction, being overwhelmed, and blending with similar objects. // ISk_7 //
"Because of excessive distance," and so forth;
just as there is no perception of a bird that has flown too far away.
Regarding the phrase "due to proximity" (*sāmīpyāt*):
the word *ati-* should also be applied here;
thus, it means "due to extreme proximity" (*atisāmīpyāt*).
Just as in the case of collyrium applied to the eye,
in both instances there is non-perception caused by a defect in the location.
Regarding the phrase "due to the impairment of the sense organs" (*indriyaghātāt*):
it refers to the non-perception of objects such as sound by the sensory organs (*buddhīndriya*), such as the ear, even when those objects are situated in a suitable location and free from defects.
‘Because the mind is unstable’;
the instability of the mind is its lack of composure,
due to its engagement with other objects.
Consequently, even when the sense-faculties are unimpaired, one does not perceive an object that is present;
in both cases, non-perception results from a defect in the sense-faculty. Since the mind is also a sense-faculty, it is mentioned separately for the sake of emphasizing its preeminence.
"Because of subtlety";
that is, because of the defect inherent in the object.
The object itself, such as an atom (*paramāṇu*) and so forth, is likewise [subtle].
By which [object], even with an undisturbed mind and unimpaired senses, it is not perceived.
"Because of intervention";
that is to say, because they are concealed by curtains and the like, even large objects such as jars are not perceived when they are not drawn near.
Regarding the term "abhibhavāt" (due to being overwhelmed):
because they are overwhelmed by the light of the sun, the stars are not perceived during the day.
"And because of being mixed with similar things":
because of the piling together of similar items, a single grain of rice thrown into a heap of grain is not seen;
in all three cases as well, there is non-perception due to the fault of the object being indistinguishable from others.
It is not the case that these [principles] do not exist simply because they are not perceived.
// 7 // If this is so, in what manner is there a non-perception of both *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and *puruṣa* (the self), even though they exist? To this, he says:
Its non-perception is due to its subtlety, not due to its non-existence, for it is perceived through its effects;
and that effect, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), is both similar to and dissimilar from primordial nature (prakṛti).
"Because of subtlety, there is no perception of that," and so forth.
Since there is no other possible mode [of existence], there is no perception of those two, even though they exist, due to their subtlety.
But why is it that there is no perception simply because of non-existence?

He says, "not from non-existence," because, for example, prior to the production of a jar, clay exists in the shards and so forth; because of the non-existence of a jar through its destruction; because of mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva), such as the absence of "horseness" in a cow or the absence of "cowness" in a horse; and because of absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva), such as that of the son of a barren woman.
The meaning is that there are four kinds.
If this is so, how is it understood that those two exist? To this he says: "Because they are apprehended through their effects" (*kāryatastadupalabdheḥ*).
Although both [the Primal Nature and the Spirit] were introduced here, nevertheless, by the word "that" (*tat*), the primary subject is indicated.
The meaning is that the cognition of the existence of the primary subject [Prakṛti] arises from its effect.
He will state the reason for establishing the existence of the person.
Asking "What is that effect? he says: "And that effect consists of the Great One (mahat) and the rest.
That which has the Great One—meaning the intellect (buddhi)—as its first member is the effect, extending from the Great One down to the gross elements.
That [effect] is the Pradhāna.
This manifest effect, consisting of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, belongs to one [who possesses it], because an effect cannot arise from that which lacks a cause.
"'Of the same form as primordial nature (prakṛti) and different from it.
This means that the manifest (vyakta) is both similar to and dissimilar from primordial nature (pradhāna). This will be applied later. // 8 //
Karika 9:
That effect, while being produced from its cause, is produced as something existent; or is it produced as something non-existent?
Or what is meant by "existent" or "non-existent"?
In that regard, because it would be superimposed with contradictory properties, neither existence nor non-existence is tenable.
As for "non-existent," this is the position of the Vaiśeṣikas.
Regarding this, he states the refutation:
"Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced; because there is the grasping of a material cause; because everything is not possible [from everything];
and because an efficient cause produces only that for which it has the capacity."
And because the effect exists within the cause, the effect pre-exists [in the cause].
"Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced," and so forth.
In this world, there is no production of what is non-existent,
such as the horns of a hare and the like.
That very existent substance, such as a jar and so forth, is produced by a specific cause, such as a lump of clay and so forth; it is not non-existent.
Regarding the phrase "because of the grasping of the material cause" (*upādānagrahaṇāt*):
here, that for the sake of which something is appropriated is its material cause (*upādāna*), such as sesame seeds are the material cause of oil.
Milk from curd;
if there were no oil or curd in this [mixture], how could those who desire them take hold of that material cause?
Therefore, because of the gathering of the material cause, the effect must already exist.
Otherwise, there would be the grasping of even sand and water.
"Because of the impossibility of everything arising from everything.
If the effect were non-existent [prior to its production], then everything would arise from everything;
however, this is not the case.
Therefore, the effect is indeed existent.
"Because that which is capable produces what is possible"—
thus it should be understood that a cause is capable, not incapable;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a sprout arising from a seed whose capacity has been impaired.
And who ought to be capable?
One who possesses power; because that possessor of power effects what is possible.
The meaning is: because of the production of an effect that is capable [of being produced].
And in this way, that which is capable would exist if it were already present in its cause in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*).
Therefore, only what exists is produced, not what does not exist.
"And because of the existence of the cause";
this means because of the existence of the cause.
If the effect were non-existent [prior to production], why would the existence of the effect occur by way of the existence of the cause?
And it is so; therefore, it is understood that it exists in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*).
Alternatively, "because of the state of being a cause" means because of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the cause.
Whatever is the nature of the cause, that is the nature of the effect;
just as from sesame seeds, which have an oily nature, oil itself emerges as oily,
and a jar has an earthy nature because its material cause is earth.
If the effect were non-existent, it would indeed arise from things that are non-existent by nature; thus, for the Sāṃkhyas, the established tenet is that only what exists arises. // 9 // Kārikā 10:

Having thus established that the effects, such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, arise as something existent, he demonstrates how they are both dissimilar and similar to primordial nature (prakṛti).
Regarding those, with reference to their dissimilarity to primordial nature, he says:
"The effect is caused, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, and indicative."
The Manifest is composed of parts and is dependent; the Unmanifest is the opposite.
"Having a cause," and so forth.
The manifest (vyakta) extends from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the primary elements (bhūta).
The unmanifest (avyakta) is the Primal Nature (pradhāna). Among these, the manifest has a cause.
Because they arise from their respective causes:
therein, the Great One (mahat) arising from Pradhāna has a cause;
the Ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) arising from the Great One has a cause.

The meaning is that from the *ahaṃkāra*, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the eleven organs arise as having causes; and from the subtle elements, the gross elements (*mahābhūta*) arise as having causes. Conversely, the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) is without cause.
Because it does not arise from anything else whatsoever;
for there is nothing other than the *pradhāna* from which it could arise.
The manifest is impermanent because it has arisen from causes, like a jar and so forth;
and the causes are exactly those previously mentioned.
The unmanifest is the opposite [of the manifest], meaning it is eternal,
because it has not arisen from anything whatsoever.
"Non-pervasive" means that the manifest is localized;
it consists of the divine, the human, and the animal realms,
because at that time it does not exist elsewhere.
"Omnipresent" (sarvagata) means the opposite [of limited], that is, unmanifest and pervasive, because it exists at all times within the three worlds, beginning with the realm of the gods.
"Active" (sakriya); thus [it is said].
In this context, by the word "action" (kriyā), transmigratory existence (saṃsaraṇa) is intended,
not mere action alone.
The meaning is that the manifest (vyakta), from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the subtle elements (sūkṣma), transmigrates as gods and so forth.
The unmanifest is the opposite [of the manifest]: it does not transmigrate.
Because it abides within the three worlds, it does not transmigrate.
Furthermore, it is "inactive" (niṣkriya) in the sense that it is not the case that activity itself is non-existent.
Because he is the creator of the world.
The Manifest is manifold, because it consists of twenty-three types, ranging from Mahat down to the gross elements.
The Manifest is the opposite [of the Unmanifest].
Because he alone is the cause of the three worlds.
Regarding the term "dependent" (*āśritam*):
whatever manifest entity, such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth, has arisen from something, that very thing is its support, and nothing else.
This statement is made for the purpose of showing that what has arisen is dependent upon another.
Otherwise, by the very term "having a cause," that which is dependent is already established;
the opposite is the unmanifest (avyakta), which is non-dependent,
because there exists no other cause besides it.
"Liṅga"; thus [it is defined]. It is called *liṅga* because by means of it the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is indicated (*liṅgyate*).
The unmanifest is the opposite, for nothing whatsoever is indicated by it.
Alternatively, it is called *liṅga* because it undergoes dissolution (*laya*).

For at the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), the five elements beginning with space dissolve, respectively, into the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) of sound and so forth; and the subtle elements and the sense organs dissolve into the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
Egoity [resides] in the Great One,
and the Great One [resides] in the Pradhāna;
the Unmanifest is the reverse.
This does not dissolve anywhere, because it is without cause.
"It has parts" (*sāvayava*):
sound and the other [elements] are called "parts.
By them, the manifest (*vyakta*)—both internal and external—is joined.
The unmanifest is the opposite, because it is not joined with them.
It is dependent (*paratantra*),
not independent (*svatantra*);
this is for the purpose of showing that whatever arises from it produces its own effect by conforming to that very [cause], and not apart from it.
Otherwise, by the very term "having a cause" (hetumat), dependence (paratantratva) is already established.
The opposite is the Unmanifest (avyakta), which is independent (svatantra) and does not depend on anything at all. // 10 //
Concerning similarity (*sārūpya*), it is said [in the *Kārikā*]:
"It consists of the three *guṇas*, is non-discriminating, is an object, is common, is insentient, and has the nature of productivity."
The Manifested is thus; likewise is the Primal Nature (pradhāna);
and the Person (puruṣa) is the opposite of that and also thus.
"Consisting of the three qualities" (*triguṇa*), and so forth:
that which possesses the three qualities, namely *sattva* and the others, is the manifest (*vyakta*) as consisting of the three qualities.
Likewise, the primary cause (*pradhāna*) is also "consisting of the three qualities," because it has that as its nature.
"Non-discriminating":
the manifest is of a non-discriminating nature because it is insentient.
Or rather, it is non-discriminative because it lacks any separateness from the qualities;
the Pradhāna is likewise.
The universal (sāmānya) is manifest,
because it is enjoyed by all persons, like a courtesan;
so too is the Pradhāna.
The manifest is insentient;
the meaning is that it does not experience pleasure, pain, or delusion.
The same applies to the Pradhāna as well.
Regarding the term "prasavadharmi":
that which possesses the property of production (prasava) is "prasavadharmi," meaning it is manifest;
the Pradhāna is likewise.
Both possess the nature of being productive.

And so, just as there is both dissimilarity and similarity between the manifest and the unmanifest—due to the nature of the Great Principle (mahat) arising from Pradhāna, and the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) arising from the Great Principle, and so forth, which involves the production of their own effects—the author asks:
"Is it the same for the Puruṣa? He replies: "The Puruṣa is the reverse of that, and likewise."
The meaning is that [the Self] is distinct from both the manifest and the unmanifest by certain attributes.
Here, the meaning of the preceding Āryā verse is applied:
the manifest possesses a cause,
while the unmanifest is without a cause.
The person (puruṣa) is also without cause, because it is not produced from anything whatsoever.
The manifest is impermanent; the unmanifest is permanent.
The Puruṣa is permanent.
Because it has not arisen from anything whatsoever.
The manifest is non-pervasive, while the unmanifest is pervasive;
likewise, the Puruṣa is pervasive when liberated from Prakṛti.
If it were joined [to the unmanifest], it would be similar to the manifest and not to the Pradhāna;
for [the manifest] always proceeds among the gods and others.
The manifest is active, while the unmanifest is inactive,
because it is not subject to transmigratory existence.
The person (puruṣa) is also inactive,
because of the absence of agency.
The manifest is manifold, while the unmanifest is one;
the Puruṣa is manifold because of its plurality.
He will demonstrate its multiplicity;
here, the dissimilarity is based on the primary factor, because that [primary factor] is one.
The manifest is dependent, while the unmanifest is independent;
the Puruṣa, too, is independent because he is not produced from anything whatsoever.
The manifest is the *liṅga*; the unmanifest is the *aliṅga*.
The *puruṣa* is also *aliṅga*.
Nothing is characterized by this, nor is it ever characterized by anything, because it is unarisen.
The manifest is possessed of parts, while the unmanifest is partless;
the Puruṣa, too, is partless because he is not joined with sound and the other objects of sense.
The dependent is manifest, while the autonomous is unmanifest;
the Puruṣa, too, is autonomous.
Because it has not arisen from anything whatsoever.
The meaning of the second noble verse is applied as follows:
the manifest and the unmanifest possess the three qualities (triguṇa), whereas the Puruṣa is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Because of the absence of qualities therein.
The manifest and the unmanifest are non-discriminative;
the Puruṣa is discriminative because of his sentience,
or rather, he is distinct because of his being devoid of qualities.
The object consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
The Puruṣa is devoid of objects;
because he is the enjoyer, he is not the enjoyed.
The universal is both manifest and unmanifest.
The Puruṣa is not universal,
because he is not an object [of cognition].
The manifest and the unmanifest are insentient;
the person (puruṣa) is sentient because of being the experiencer of pleasure and so forth.
The manifest and the unmanifest possess the quality of productivity;
the Puruṣa does not possess the quality of productivity, because he is not an agent. Thus it has been said. // 11 //
Regarding the statement that there are three qualities (*triguṇa*) because there are both dissimilarity and similarity among the three, [the author] asks:
which are the three qualities, and what is their nature? He says:

The guṇas consist of pleasure, pain, and dejection; they serve the purposes of illumination, activity, and restraint; and they function through mutual suppression, support, production, and union. (ISK 12)
"Consisting of pleasure, pain, and dejection," and so forth.
Those qualities whose natures (*ātman*) are pleasure and the rest are described as such; these are the three qualities (*guṇas*), namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
Among them, *sattva* consists of pleasure, that is, its nature is happiness.
Rajas has the nature of dissatisfaction and the nature of suffering;
tamas has the nature of despondency and the nature of delusion.
For the qualities (guṇas), being beyond the reach of the senses, are inferred through their transformations such as pleasure and so forth, and are therefore designated as having those natures.
Furthermore, he states what their purpose is: "They have illumination, activity, and restraint as their purposes.
Sattva exists for the purpose of illumination because it is luminous;
rajas exists for the purpose of activity because it is mobile.
It is for the purpose of restriction, because [the mind] is motionless due to darkness.
To address whether these qualities (*guṇas*) depend upon one another or not, he says: "The qualities function through mutual suppression, support, production, and companionship.
The word "mutual" (*anyo 'nya*) is connected with each [term].
"Suppression" (*abhibhava*) means the act of suppressing.
The suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *pacādyac*.
"Mutual overcoming" (*anyo'nyābhibhavāḥ*) means the overcoming of one by another.
For example, among the gods, when the quality of *sattva* is predominant, it overcomes *rajas* and *tamas*.
Among humans, there are passion (rajas), purity (sattva), and darkness (tamas); among animals, [there are] darkness, purity, and passion.
They are called "bases" (āśraya) because they are resorted to.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a verbal root.
They are mutual supports,
like a tripod of three staffs.
They have no other substratum,
and as agents they are themselves without a substratum;
they are called "producers" because they bring things into existence.
According to the rule "kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam," the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
Furthermore, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, they should be understood here as having the sense of "making known" (*bodhana*).
The meaning is that they are mutual awakeners.
For every manifest entity being produced is produced as consisting of the three guṇas;
therein, when sattva is predominant, then rajas and tamas have their powers suppressed.
It has been stated that, like a magnet, it awakens [the sattva] as iron is awakened;
by means of a quality produced by another, it brings about manifestation.
The same should be applied to rajas and tamas.
When two qualities have their powers manifested, then each of them overcomes the other;
that is to say, it awakens it.
This is what is meant by "they are mutual consorts."
The meaning is that they are mutual companions.
And so it has been said in the *Viṣṇugītā*:
"Sattva is the mate of rajas; rajas is the mate of sattva."
The union of both the qualities of sattva and rajas is called tamas.
Since it is evident that when one individual manifestation is mentioned, the three [guṇas] are implied by their mutual suppression and awakening,
the author says "mutually functioning" (anyo 'nyavṛttayaḥ) to show that the other two likewise produce activity.
"Functioning" (vṛttiḥ) means transformation into the form of pleasure and so forth.
They are called "modes" (*vṛtti*) because they are the causes of modes;
the meaning is that they are mutual causes of one another's modes.
For example, there might be a certain woman who possesses supreme qualities of beauty and character.

Because it is white (pure), that [quality] is *sāttvika*; it produces happiness for her husband, while for some co-wives it produces suffering and for others despondency—in this case, *sattva* is the cause of the activity of both herself and the two [others].
Because a certain lord is exceedingly brave, his servants are *rājasa*;
they produce suffering through their blows for others who are fighting.
In this case, *rajas* is the cause of the activity of both the self and the two [others]: it causes despondency in those fleeing and satisfaction in the master;
and by making the clouds dark with water... due to their height.

The *tāmasa* clouds, while raining, produce despondency in women whose husbands are away, sorrow for travelers, but joy for farmers; thus, in this case, *tamas* is the cause of the activity of itself and of two other factors. // 12 // *Kārikā 13*
Regarding these ill-defined characteristics, he states another definition:
"Sattva is light and illuminating; rajas is stimulating and mobile; tamas is heavy and enveloping."
And its functioning is, in terms of its actual meaning, like that of a lamp.
"Sattva," and so forth.
The teachers of Sāṃkhya maintain that *sattva* is light by nature and luminous;
through its predominance, the limbs of the body become light.
The sense organs are capable of illuminating their respective objects;
and external substances become light, luminous in nature, and pure.
"Rajas is stimulating and mobile.
It is called "stimulating" (upaṣṭambhaka) because it stimulates.
Due to its predominance, Devadatta exerts himself.
The mind becomes restless,
and external objects become restless as well.
"Darkness is indeed the act of veiling"; it veils, that is, it covers. [This is explained by the rule:
"The kṛtya and lyuṭ suffixes occur diversely."
Thus, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used either in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) or the instrument (*karaṇe*);
subsequently, the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).
Due to the excess of this [element], the limbs become heavy.
And the sense faculties are seized by darkness itself; they become dull and impure.
This is merely an illustration; other [examples] should also be understood.
And so they have said: "Affection, joy, attachment, lightness, serenity, and gladness..."
Stolidity, agitation, aversion, movement, drying up, burning heat, and fragmentation;
as well as obstruction, destruction, depression, heaviness, dejection, and fear—these are to be known respectively as the marks of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas.

But one might ask: "Since these qualities are mutually distinct and contradictory, how can they exist together in one place? To this he says: "And their functioning is for the sake of the purpose, like a lamp" (*pradīpavaccārthato vṛttiḥ*). "Like a lamp" means as in the case of a lamp.
A lamp is a composite of oil, a wick, and fire.
Just as there is the activity of a lamp and other such things— which, though mutually distinct, constitute a collective whole—
toward objects like jars situated in darkness that are to be illuminated by Devadatta,
so too is the activity of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* for the sake of the purpose of the *puruṣa*.
And [the means of proof are] the perception of the word "puruṣārtha" (the purpose of the Spirit).
// 13 // Now, an objection: But has it not been stated that "The Manifested is composed of the three guṇas, non-discriminative, objective, common, insentient, and productive"?
In that regard, since pleasure, pain, and delusion are perceived, the manifest (vyakta) is established as being composed of the three guṇas.
To the question of how the properties beginning with non-discrimination (aviveki) and ending with productivity (prasava) are established, he says:
"The [properties] beginning with non-discrimination are established because of the presence of the three guṇas and because of the absence of their opposites."
Because the effect consists of the qualities of its cause, the unmanifest is also established.
"Non-discrimination and so forth are established," and so on.
This is a designation of the qualities by way of the possessor of the qualities.
Non-discrimination and the other qualities are established.
The words "the manifest" complete the sentence.
Why? Because of the three qualities (traiguṇya).
How so? Because the qualities themselves are non-discriminating, objects of experience, common, insentient, and productive;
and since these are established in the manifest (vyakta), the existence of the qualities is proven.
"Because of the absence of its opposite";
that is, because of the absence of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*).
Since the qualities of non-discrimination and so forth are absent when the three qualities are absent.
For non-discrimination and the other qualities cannot belong to a Puruṣa who is devoid of attributes (nirguṇa).
Therefore, non-discrimination and the rest are established as arising solely from the three guṇas.
This being the case, it is established that the Pradhāna is likewise characterized by the three guṇas.
As it has been said: "Because the effect consists of the qualities of its cause, the Unmanifest (avyakta) is also established [as having those qualities]."
That which is the quality of the cause is its essence (ātman), its intrinsic nature (svabhāva); that which possesses this is so described.
Its intrinsic nature is its reality (tattva).
Therefore, in this world, it is observed that an effect possesses the qualities of its cause.
A cloth produced from white or black threads is itself white or black;
if the unmanifest were not of such a nature, how could the manifest be of such a nature? (14)
Kārikā 15:
Now, it may be objected that attributes are considered only when a substratum exists;
since the primary substratum itself has not yet been established, how can one speak of its being "non-discriminative" and so forth? To this, he says:

Because of the finite measure of differentiated objects, because of their homogeneity, because of their activity proceeding from a capacity, because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-differentiation of the manifold universe [at its origin]. // ISk_15 //
"Of the differentiated effects" (*bhedānām*), and so forth.

Since it has already been established by the statement "the Great One (*mahat*) and the rest are effects because they are perceived as such," the immediately following phrase is introduced for the sake of further reinforcement once this has been correctly understood.
They are called "differentiated effects" (*bhedāḥ*) because they are differentiated; that is, specific effects. Of these, [one common cause is observed].
And because of their limited extent;
the meaning is that the various particulars are finite.
And that by which they are delimited is observed to be a single common substrate for them.
Just as rice is the [common] designation for the various stages of its development—root, sprout, leaf, stalk, bud, flower, and grain—so too are there external and internal varieties.
The limited external varieties consist of fourteen, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass;

the internal varieties consist of twenty-three, namely: the Great Principle (mahat), ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra), the subtle elements (tanmātra), the sense organs (indriya), and the gross elements (bhūta).
Therefore, these [effects] must have one common correlate;
that in which they correlate exists as the unmanifest cause—this is an inference based on general observation (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa).
"Because of the pervasive presence" (*samanvayāt*);
the word "of the particulars" (*bhedānām*) is understood to carry over.
"Pervasive presence" (*samanvaya*) means "concomitance" (*anugama*).
The meaning is "because they follow from a single genus.
It is observed that for those particulars which follow from a single genus, there is one and the same cause of that nature;
just as a lump of gold is the cause of bracelets, armlets, and so forth.

Or, just as a lump of clay is the material cause of bowls and the like, so too, because these external and internal things are permeated by pleasure, pain, and delusion, they must have a single such cause.
That which is their aggregate is the Pradhāna; this is an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
"And because activity proceeds from power.
Here, it is observed that the activity of jars and the like is preceded by the power of the potter and others, not by a lack of power.
The activity of these [beings], both external and internal, is likewise observed.
Furthermore, prior to its manifestation, there must exist a potency produced by that which is yet to arise;
that very potency attains the state of being unmanifest—this is the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
Regarding the phrase "due to the distinction between cause and effect" (*kāraṇakāryavibhāgāt*):
the word for "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is placed first because it precedes [the effect] in time;
however, the rule that the word with fewer syllables (*alpāctara*) should be placed first is not absolute.
That from which something arises is the cause,
and that which arises is the effect.
For example, the distinction between a lump of clay and a jar is observed through their relationship as producer and produced, and because they perform different purposeful actions.
Otherwise, the function of carrying water which belongs to a jar does not belong to a lump of clay,
and that which belongs to a lump of clay does not belong to a jar;
likewise, because the manifest— such as the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth— is an effect and performs distinct purposeful actions, there is a distinction between them.
Therefore, it must have a cause;
and what else could that cause be other than the Unmanifest?

In this commentary, because [the point] is already established by the statement, "The Great One and so forth are effects, since they are perceived through their being effects," others explain it differently:
that which assists is the cause (*kāraṇa*).
That which is assisted is the effect (*kārya*), because of the distinction between those two;
that is to say, due to the relationship of the benefactor and the beneficiary.
In that regard, the body-residing [factors] such as the *kārya*... assist the causes through their locations, means, and enjoyments.
And the causes [of the earth] are to be understood through its growth, the healing of wounds, and its preservation.
Furthermore, external causes assist one another through the earth’s functions of supporting, cohesion, transformation, expansion, and providing space.
Likewise, divine, human, and animal beings are mutually supportive of one another.
In this regard, the divine— namely, the timely arrival of cold, heat, and rain—
benefits humans and animals.
He protects the human through sacrifices, offerings, and hymns; he assists the divine through nourishment and medicines; and he benefits those of animal birth through various means.
Just as the relationship between internal and external things appears to be produced by intelligence, so too must there be some ordainer of this [universe].
From what does this distinction arise? It arises from the impossibility of its being otherwise.
"Because of the non-differentiation of the manifold form.
That which has no differentiation is "non-differentiated" (avibhāga);
the meaning is "undivided."
Therefore, the remainder of the argument is "because of the perception of manifoldness.

In this world, a variety of forms—a diversity such as juice, inspissated juice, molasses, candied sugar, and granulated sugar—is seen to arise from a single, undivided substance; likewise, a manifoldness consisting of curd, whey, butter, clarified butter, and so forth, is perceived to arise from a single substance, milk.
Thus, there is a manifold variety of internal and external things;
therefore, they must exist as undifferentiated from one another—this is the inference based on general observation (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa).
But another says: "In the non-differentiation of the manifoldness (vaiśvarūpya). Non-differentiation is dissolution; the manifoldness is the world, because it possesses diverse forms.
At the time of dissolution, where does the manifold diversity of the world dissolve, given that there are the states of persistence, origination, and dissolution of the universe?
Furthermore, dissolution into the Lord is not possible,
because He is accepted as being devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Therefore, by the principle of "otherwise it would be impossible," that one [Primal Substance] exists.
And so they have said: "From Pradhāna, in successive order, comes the creation and the transmigration of the world."
"Moving again in that very same place in reverse order.
(15) To explain the purpose of setting these causes in motion, he says: [Kārikā 16]
The unmanifest exists as the cause; it proceeds from the three qualities and from their aggregation;
it evolves like water.
Because of the specific distinction based on each respective quality and its substratum.
"There is a cause," and so forth.
If the unmanifest (avyakta) exists as the cause, how does it proceed? To this he says: "Because of the three qualities (guṇas) and because of their collective emergence.
This means that when the qualities residing in primordial nature (prakṛti) proceed in a state of equilibrium, they proceed by taking all three into account, not just one by one;
whereas when they proceed in a state of disequilibrium, [they proceed accordingly].
An effect proceeds from its arising because it is originated by causes;
the meaning is that it refers to that quality whose emergence is universal, since the powers of all other [qualities] are eclipsed.
If the unmanifest proceeds from the collection, then that which has arisen from it does not become unmanifest.
He says, "By transformation," and so forth, [meaning] that from white or black threads, a white or black cloth comes into being;
"transformation" (pariṇāma) is the becoming of another state from a previous state.
From that cause it proceeds:
just as from a tiny seed a great forest tree, with its roots, branches, and sub-branches fully developed, becomes manifest,
so too does the manifest evolve from the unmanifest.

If this is so, one might ask: how can the three worlds, which have arisen from a single form, possess manifold forms? To this he says: "Because of the distinction of the substrata of the respective qualities, like water" (*salilavatpratipratiguṇāśrayaviśeṣāt*). It exists similarly to water, thus it is "like water" (*salilavat*). The qualities with respect to each [element] are "the respective qualities" (*pratipratiguṇāḥ*).
These very [evolutes] proceed from that specific distinction which constitutes their respective substrata.

Just as water, though possessing a single taste when originating from the atmosphere, comes to possess various tastes due to the specific distinctions of the substrata of individual qualities such as pungent or sour, so too does the Unmanifest (avyakta), being composed of the gunas, proceed in manifold forms due to the specific distinctions of the substrata of each individual guna.
In that regard, due to the specific nature of the substrate of *sattva*, one exists in the state of a deity; due to the specific nature of the substrate of *rajas*, in the state of a human;
and due to the specific nature of the substrate of *tamas*, in the state of an animal womb. // 16 //

Kārikā 17: Having thus established the existence and the activity of the Unmanifest (avyakta), he speaks in order to establish the existence of the Spirit (puruṣa): "Because composite objects exist for the sake of another; because of the reversal of the three attributes (guṇas) and so forth; because of superintendence;"
The Puruṣa exists because there must be an experiencer and because of the activity directed toward the goal of isolation (kaivalya).
"Because of being a composite for the sake of another," and so forth.
That which is composed is a "composite" (*saṃghāta*).
Being both a composite and for the sake of another is "a composite for the sake of another" (*saṃghātaparārtha*).
The state of being a composite is the reason (*hetu*), and being for the sake of another is the probandum (*sādhya*).
In this world, those things such as beds and seats which are outside the category of composites are seen to be for the sake of another;
for they serve the purpose of another, such as Devadatta, and not their own purpose.
These internal aggregates, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and designated as the body, must exist for the sake of another;
yet there is no other "another" apart from the Puruṣa.
The Person alone is supreme; everything else is seen by another.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the person (puruṣa) is nothing other than the body itself, which extends from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the primary elements? To this, he says: "Because of the reversal of the three qualities and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the five attributes beginning with non-discrimination (aviveki) are indicated. For it has been stated that the person is the opposite of those [attributes].
Furthermore, because the person (puruṣa) is the opposite of that [primordial matter], how could the person be merely the principles beginning with the Great One (mahat)?
Therefore, the person is distinct [from them], for whose sake these aggregates exist.
Regarding the term "adhiṣṭhānāt":
that in which something presides is called an *adhiṣṭhāna*.
It is observed in this world that the body, extending from the Great Principle (*mahat*) down to the primary elements (*bhūta*), being an *adhiṣṭhāna*, is presided over by another.
Just as in the case of a chariot and so forth,
the body is observed to be an instrument;
therefore, it must have a controller.
That which is the controller is the Puruṣa;
the internal organ is not the controller because it is insentient— this is an inference based on general observation (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa).
"Because of being an enjoyer";
this means "because of being an experiencer.
In this world, having perceived an object of enjoyment, an enjoyer is inferred.

The object of enjoyment, beginning with the Mahat and ending with the gross elements, is perceived; therefore, it must have an enjoyer—this is an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
Furthermore, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is not the enjoyer.

Because that [body] is insentient and is an object of experience, he who is the experiencer is indeed the *puruṣa*. The living body possesses a self (*sātmaka*), because it possesses vital breaths and so forth.
Within this body, this self is accompanied by many other entities of the same class.
Because it is associated with specific births and so forth, like the mind.
"And because activity is for the sake of isolation (kaivalya).
Isolation means liberation.
This activity belongs to one whose primary aim is something other than that [liberation].
For instance: primordial matter (pradhāna) transforms into the nature of the intellect (buddhi); from the intellect arise the eighteen [faculties];
and among those, knowledge is isolation (kaivalya).
In that regard, if the Puruṣa did not exist, then activity for his sake would not occur;
therefore, the Puruṣa exists because [activity] cannot otherwise be accounted for.
Regarding that established self (*puruṣa*), there are disputes:
some maintain that this single person resides within all bodies;
others hold that all embodied beings possess multiple selves because they are endowed with a self-nature.
Regarding the multitude of the bodies of yogis, others maintain that there is a distinct person (puruṣa) in each body.
The Vedāntins, however, hold that there is only one ancient Person; from him, like sparks from a fire, the persons in each body have manifested. 17.
Kārikā 18:
Here it is said:
Because there is a specific determination of birth, death, and the sense organs, and because they do not function simultaneously.
The plurality of persons is established also from the diversity of the three qualities.
"Of birth, death, and the instruments," and so forth.
The "instrument" (karaṇa) refers to the sense organs such as the eye; birth and destruction pertain to the body, the senses, and their substratum.
Through association with these, the person (puruṣa) is likewise designated as being born and dying.
These two do not occur for the Self (*puruṣa*) by its own nature.
Why? Because of its eternity. In that regard, if there were only one *puruṣa*, then when one [individual] is born or dies, there would be birth and death for all;
likewise, when one possesses sight or hearing, all would be sighted (or hearing) [and when one is blind (or deaf), all would be blind (or deaf)].
Whether they were to see or hear, it would be the same as if there were only one person who was blind or deaf.
But this is not so, because birth and the rest are restricted [to specific individuals].
Therefore, the plurality of puruṣas is established through the principle of "otherwise it would be impossible" (anyathānupapatti).
"And because of the non-simultaneous occurrence [of activity]"—

if there were only one person, then when activity regarding merit and demerit, gain and loss, or pleasure and pain occurs within the body while presided over by that single controller, [the results would have to occur simultaneously].
All [causes] would indeed function simultaneously;
since this is not the case, there is the impossibility of any other [explanation].
"And because of the reversal of the three qualities. Here, "the three qualities" (*triguṇya*) refers to the three qualities themselves.
Their "reversal" (*viparyaya*) means their alteration or change of state.

Because the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) consists of the three *guṇas*, the *puruṣa* is also said to consist of the three *guṇas* due to its association with that substrate. In that case, if there were only one *puruṣa*, then when one [individual] is of a *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, or *tāmasa* nature,
all would necessarily be of that same kind.
But this is not the case, because the qualities are seen to be the opposite; thus, there is an inconsistency otherwise.
Even in this view—that individual persons (puruṣas) emerge from the Primeval Person (purāṇapuruṣa) like sparks from fire—there is indeed a plurality of persons.

Because they are distinct from one another, there are two perspectives: whether they are non-different or different from the Primeval Person. Since that has been examined elsewhere, we have not set it forth here for fear of making the text too cumbersome. // 18 //
Kārikā 19:
Having thus established the plurality of the Puruṣas, he speaks in order to describe their attributes:
"And from this very [absence of] error, the witness-status of this Puruṣa is established."
Isolation consists in neutrality, the state of being a witness, and the absence of agency.
"And from that reversal," and so forth.

From that reversal which was previously stated— namely, "consisting of the three guṇas, non-discriminative, objective," and so on— the attributes of the Puruṣa, such as being a witness and the like, are established.
In that regard, because the qualityless *puruṣa* possesses the nature of non-procreation, it is a non-agent;
and he who is a non-agent is indifferent.
His indifference is sevenfold.
And so it has been said:
"He sees, he hears, he does everything, yet he undergoes neither persistence nor involvement;
[he arises] neither from himself, nor from another, nor from both, but is indifferent."
And he who is indifferent becomes a witness as well, because the entire complex of actions belonging to the primary agent is devoid of [subjective] qualities.
Isolation results from the state of being absolute; and because of its consciousness, it possesses the nature of being a seer.
But if he is not an agent, how can it be said that "the person exists because of being an experiencer"? For they have said:
"Just as children, fire, and trees are indeed experiencers of things not created by themselves."
The person, moreover, is likewise the enjoyer of the fruits of objects, even though he himself has not created them. Thus it is said.
Thus it has been stated that this [unmanifest] possesses the quality of being an enjoyer even though it is not an agent. [Objection:
But if the unmanifest is insentient, how does it proceed toward the body, the sense organs, and the designation [of the self] as its substratum for the sake of merit, demerit, and so forth?
Because that [Pradhāna] is insentient, he says:
"Therefore, through conjunction with that, the insentient linga appears as if it were sentient;
likewise, although the gunas are the agents, the indifferent one (the Puruṣa) appears as if he were the agent. (ISk 20)
"From that, due to its conjunction with that," and so forth.
From that conjunction which occurs between that [Prakṛti] and the Puruṣa, the insentient appears as if it were sentient,
just as iron is said to be "fire" due to conjunction with fire.
He will explain the *liṅga* (the subtle body), which extends from the Great Principle (*mahat*) down to the subtle elements (*sūkṣma*).

If that very [Prakṛti], consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), is the agent and not the Person (puruṣa), how is it said that "the Person goes"? To this he says: "Even though the agency belongs to the qualities, the indifferent one appears as if he were the agent. Thus, the agency belongs to the qualities, not to the Person.
Just as the insentient *liṅga* becomes as if sentient through conjunction with the Puruṣa,
so too, though being a non-agent, it becomes as if an agent through conjunction with the *liṅga* composed of the *guṇas*;
it remains indifferent.
Just as a master, though not himself a warrior, is designated as "a warrior" due to his association with warriors who are his servants, so too the *puruṣa* is metaphorically called the "agent.
And thus it has been said:

"Overpowered by *tamas* and possessing perverted vision, the ignorant man, though lacking the power even to bend a blade of grass, falsely imagines: 'I am the doer,' regarding these qualities of *prakṛti* as they proceed. (20) Kārikā 21:
Now, is the conjunction of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*) solely for the sake of consciousness (*caitanya*),
or is it also for another purpose? To this he says:
For the sake of the Spirit's perception and for the sake of the Primal Matter's isolation, there is a union of both, like that of the lame man and the blind man; from this union, creation proceeds.
"Of the person," and so forth.
The purpose of the person is twofold:
the enjoyment of objects and isolation (kaivalya).
Both of these must be accomplished by means of Pradhāna;
and since the enjoyment of objects is not possible without the sovereign power of Pradhāna,
the Puruṣa unites with Pradhāna for the purpose of vision.
Pride (māna) is joined with the Person (puruṣa) because it is unable to display its own power;
having seen and experienced all that power, the Person becomes dispassionate due to its insipidity and is abandoned by Primordial Matter (pradhāna).

For one who has been abandoned, there is isolation (kaivalya); therefore, the conjunction of both is for the sake of vision and for the sake of isolation, like the fish and the water, or the gnat and the udumbara fruit.
"Like the lame and the blind":
this is the illustration.
The lame man, though possessing sight, sees the path but does not travel upon it.
Even a blind man can move about, though he does not see the path;
between those two who had lost their own purpose, a connection was formed for the sake of reaching the village.
Therein, the lame man, having climbed onto the shoulder of the blind man, became possessed of movement.

Even a blind man becomes possessed of sight through the presence of one who can see; yet there is a separation between those two once they have reached the village. In the same way, the inactive Puruṣa, having conjoined with Pradhāna, wanders among the gods and other realms in order to behold its manifestations.

Although primordial matter (pradhāna) is insentient, through the superintendence of the Spirit (puruṣa), it acts as if it were sentient and accomplishes both [the creation and liberation of the world].
Therefore, the conjunction of both is like that of the lame man and the blind man.
But how can there be perception and isolation through mere conjunction alone? To this he says: "The creation is caused by that.
The meaning is that the production of the group beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) is brought about by conjunction. // 21 // Kārikā 22:
Demonstrating that very point, he says:

"From primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat); from that, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); from that, the group of sixteen; and from five among that group of sixteen, the five gross elements arise. (ISk 22)
"From *prakṛti* arises the Great One (*mahān*)," and so forth.
*Prakṛti*, *pradhāna*, *kāraṇa*, *avyakta*, *guṇasāmya*, *tamobahula*, and *avyākṛta* are synonyms for *prakṛti*.
From that, the Great One (*mahān*) is produced, and it is characterized by an abundance of *tamas*.
"Intellect," "understanding," "cognition," "conviction," and "apprehension" are synonyms for *buddhi*.
From that, the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) arises;
it is, however, abundant in *rajas* and *tamas*.
Ahaṃkāra, suparṇapaṇi,
and tatpuruṣa are synonyms for ahaṃkāra.
"Therefore, the group of sixteen [arises]";
this means that from that ego (ahaṅkāra), the group of sixteen is produced—
namely, the eleven organs and the five subtle elements (tanmātra).
"Those *hṛṣīkāṇi* are synonyms for *indriyāṇi* (the senses).
Subtle, superior, and minute (*aṇavaḥ*) [objects] are the *tanmātras*; these are their synonyms."
"Therefore, from that group of sixteen, from five [of them], the five gross elements arise.

This means that from the group of sixteen, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) emerge first; from these, by an increase of one [attribute] at a time, the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*) come into being.
Among these, from the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*), space (*ākāśa*) arises, possessing a single attribute.
From the subtle element of touch conjoined with the subtle element of sound, wind arises as twofold;
from the subtle element of form conjoined with those two, fire arises as threefold;
and from the subtle element of taste conjoined with those [three], water arises as fourfold.
From the subtle element of smell, conjoined with four [other subtle elements], earth arises as possessing five qualities.
By these, the gross specific manifestations (viśeṣas) beginning with the eleven organs are designated;
within these, the twenty-four principles (tattvas) find their culmination. // 22 //
Kārikā 23:
He states the definition of the intellect (buddhi): "The intellect is determination; its qualities are virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty."
This form is characterized by sattva; that which is contrary to it is characterized by tamas.
"Adhyavasāya," and so forth.
This term "adhyavasāya" regarding objects such as sound refers to the definition of right cognition (*subuddhi*), up to [the point where one determines] "this is fragrance.
And that [right cognition] has eight forms.

"Dharma is knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty. In this context, that determination which consists of the practice directed toward no [external] object is dharma; it comprises the five restraints (yamas) and the observances (niyamas).
As it is stated in the *Sāṃkhyapravacana*: "Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the *yamas*";
"Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the *niyamas*.
Among these, contentment (*santoṣa*) is the lack of desire for more than what is at hand, due to the proximity of the means already available.

Austerity (*tapas*) consists of the conquest of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and the mastery of postures and means; it includes the vow of silence (*mauna*)—both the "silence of wood" (*kāṣṭha-mauna*) and the "silence of form" (*ākāra-mauna*)—as well as religious observances (*vratas*) such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*.
Self-study (*svādhyāya*) is the study of the scriptures on liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*) or the recitation of the *praṇava*.

Devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna) is the propitiation of a distinguished deity; it is so called because its practice is identical to that of those who are not subject to saṃsāra. Its opposite practice is unrighteousness (adharma).

Knowledge is the determination of the twenty-five principles (tattva) according to their own designations, characteristics, and purposes; it is the knowledge of the distinction between the qualities (guṇa) and the person (puruṣa).
Everything else is ignorance (ajñāna).
Dispassion (*virāga*) is the turning away [from objects] due to perceiving defects in sense-objects, the body, and the senses.
Attachment (*rāga*) is the desire for them. Sovereignty consists of eight qualities: *aṇimā*,...
magnificence, levity, and reach;
Irresistible will,
lordship,
and mastery.
And there is the power of determining the course of one's desires at will (*yatrakāmāvasāyitva*).
Among these, *aṇimā* is minuteness, by which quality one becomes subtle and moves about.
The term *aṇiman* is used [for the power of becoming minute] because of the metaphorical application of the cause to the effect;
this same principle should be applied to the subsequent [powers] as well.
*Laghimā* is lightness.
By which one becomes lighter than the wind;
*mahimā* is greatness, by which there is the attainment of [powers] such as *dharmā* among the worlds.

The quality by which one attains what is desired is *prākāmya* (the power of irresistible will), which is an abundance of desire; by means of this, the one is made many and the many are made one. *Īśitva* (lordship) is sovereignty, by which beings such as stationary objects become obedient to one's command.
