Mastery (*vaśitva*) is the state of being masterful (*vaśitā*), by which one acts independently;

it is the quality of abiding according to one's desire (*yatrakāmāvaśāyitva*), meaning one whose nature is to abide wherever they wish (*yatra-kāmena icchayā avaśetum śīlam yasya sa yatrakāmāvaśāyī*).
The state of that [is] "the power to abide wherever one desires" (*yatra-kāmāvaśāyitvam*).
Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *śī* functions here as *sthā* (to stand).
The meaning is that by which quality one abides in heaven, in the intermediate space, or on earth;
"this form is sāttvika" because it contains an abundance of *sattva* and *tamas*.
The meaning is that when *sattva* is predominant, these four [qualities] come into being.
Regarding the phrase "that which is *tāmasa* is the reverse of this":
the meaning is that when *tamas* is intensified, there occurs that which is the opposite of the fourfold set beginning with *dharma*, characterized by predominance.
Unrighteousness (*adharma*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*), and lack of mastery (*anaiśvarya*).
// 23 // The definition of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) is stated:
Self-conceit is the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra);
from that, the twofold creation proceeds:
the group of eleven and the pentad of subtle elements (tanmātra).
"Abhimāna," and so forth.
Abhimati is abhimāna.
Abhimāna regarding objects such as form is [the thought], "I am possessed of form."
"These objects belong to me"— this is the characteristic of the mark of "I-making" (ahaṅkāra).
Therefore, from this *ahaṅkāra*, characterized by self-conceit (*abhimāna*), "the twofold creation proceeds";
it is called *sarga* because it is created (*sṛjyate*).
In order to demonstrate that very twofold division, he says: "And the group of eleven.
That which has eleven as its measure is the "elevenfold," namely the group beginning with the sense of hearing.
"And the five subtle elements (*tanmātra-pañcaka*). The meaning is: "merely the essential nature of the subtle elements. The subtle elements are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
The mention of "the apprehension of the measure" (mātrāgrahaṇa) is for the purpose of excluding contact with the primary elements (bhūta),
because sound and other qualities are also possible within the primary elements. // 24 // Kārikā 25:
Showing that this ego (ahaṃkāra) is of three kinds, he says:
"The group of eleven, characterized by sattva, proceeds from the modified (vaikṛta) ego;
the subtle elements (tanmātra), characterized by tamas, proceed from the source of the elements (bhūtādi)."
From the taijasa [element], both [arise].

"Of the nature of *sattva*," and so forth. When *sattva* is predominant, then the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) becomes the "transformative" (*vaikṛta*) conceit; when *rajas* is predominant, it is the "radiant" (*taijasa*).
And tamas, when predominant, is called bhūtādi;
from that [bhūtādi], the group of eleven consisting of the vaikṛta proceeds,
and it is sāttvika, being abundant in sattva.
Because it grasps its own object.
From the *ahaṃkāra* of the nature of *tamas*, beginning with the element of earth (*bhūta*), arises the group of subtle elements (*tanmātra*); that is *tāmasa* because it abounds in *tamas*.
From that *tāmasa* group of subtle elements, the *tāmasa* group of gross elements (*bhūtagaṇa*) proceeds.
"From the taijasa [element], both [arise]"—
this is the intended meaning: both of these pentads proceed [from it],
because at the initial time, this [taijasa] acts as an auxiliary to both.
Both the *vaikṛta* (modified) and the *bhūtādi* (originative) [forms of ego] possess the nature of illumination and stability; therefore, they do not possess the nature of activity.
Consequently, depending upon the *taijasa* (fiery) ego, which possesses the nature of activity, as its assistant, it produced the group of eleven and the group of five [senses].
What, then, is the eleventh? He says:
the sense organs of cognition (buddhīndriya) are called the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and skin; they call the vocal organ, hands, feet, anus, and genitals the organs of action (karmendriya). ISk_26 //
"The sense organs," and so forth.
The sense organ is of two kinds.
Among these, the eye is that by which one sees.
The ear by which one hears;
the skin by which one touches;
the tongue by which one tastes.
The nose is that by which one smells;
the designation "those called [the senses]" refers to those faculties—this is a description emphasizing the names.
They are five: those called the eye, ear, skin, tongue, and nose.
The teachers of Sāṃkhya say that the "deliberation preceded by intelligence" refers to the cognitive organs (*buddhīndriya*). Here,
the order has been established according to the sequence of the words [in the sūtra],
whereas the actual order is ear, skin, and eye.
"Speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals.
These are the organs of action (karmendriya) because they bring about action.
From this very usage, it is known that the word *upastha* also exists in the masculine gender.
And that [organ] belongs to both women and men.
Among them, the organ of speech is located in the throat;
the others are well known. // 26 //
Showing the eleventh faculty, [the author] says:
"In this context, the mind possesses the nature of both."
And the faculty of volition [is distinct] due to its similarity [to the intellect];
the diversity [of objects] and external distinctions arise from the specific modifications of the guṇas.
"Here, the mind is of a dual nature," and so forth.
"Here" means in this group of sense organs, the mind is of a dual nature, that is, it possesses a twofold character.
The meaning is that at the time of grasping its respective objects, it functions as both a cognitive organ (*buddhīndriya*) and an active organ (*karmendriya*).
Because it functions in both cases, he states that this is its defining characteristic: "it conceives" means it is a conceiving faculty, [determining] "this is so, not that."
To explain how it is a faculty (*indriya*), he says: "And it is a faculty because of its similarity," and so forth.
The meaning is that it is due to its equality with the [other] faculties;
that is to say, just as the other [faculties] are signs of Indra (*indra-liṅga*), so too is the mind (*manas*).
In that regard, how is there a difference in the essential nature of those [faculties] produced from a single ego-principle (ahaṅkāra)?
That which is the sensory faculty of hearing and so forth has its own specific object and does not have the objects of others as well.
If the organs of action, such as speech and the rest, were restricted to their respective specific functions, they would not perform any other actions;
however, the mind possesses the nature of both.
He states that it is not of a single nature: "The diversity [of the elements] arises from the specific transformations of the *guṇas*.

The *guṇas*, such as *sattva* and the others, which reside in the *ahaṅkāra*, possess a specific transformation through the two doors of mutual suppression and support; it is precisely from this that their diversity arises.
For those very *guṇas* (are transformed...)
Distinguished by their respective names, they possess the designations of their sense organs and have various objects. How then is there a restriction of location and a restriction of function?
In that regard, the tactile sense organ (tvagindriya) has its function throughout the entire body, both externally and internally.
The eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are situated separately on the outside of the head and have external functions.
Speech is situated in the mouth.
And the hands and other [limbs] are situated separately below the arms; they have external objects as their domain for action.
To this he says: "And the external differences.
Those other distinctions of objects, which arise from the restriction of place and the restriction of occurrence, are also due solely to specific transformations of the *guṇas*;
there is no other intervening cause here. // 27 //
Regarding these sense organs, he states which function belongs to which:
"The function of the five [organs] with respect to sound and the other objects is held to be mere observation."
And the five [faculties] have speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure as their functions.
"In sound and so forth," etc. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are included.
Among these, the Sāṃkhya teachers maintain that the function (vṛtti) of the five sense organs, beginning with the ear, is held to be mere observation (ālocana-mātra) in their respective order.
For the ears and other senses merely perform the illumination of the object,
whereas the determination belongs to the intellect (buddhi). Indeed, it is the established tenet that the person (puruṣa) perceives the object as determined by the intellect.
The functions—the actions—of the organs of action, such as speech and the rest, are also, in their respective order: speaking, grasping, and so forth.
Among these, the function of the organ of speech is the utterance of various sounds; the function of the hands is the grasping of what is to be taken.
Movement is the traveling to another place by means of the feet;
evacuation is the discharge of the waste of food by means of the anus;
and exhilaration is joy, the bliss arising from the emission and union of semen—that is the function of the organ of generation. // 28 //
Kārikā 29: To the question "What is the function (*vṛtti*) of intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*?", he says:
The function of this triad is its own specific characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*); this indeed is their non-common [function].
The common function of the organs consists of the five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa.
"'The function is its own characteristic' (svālakṣaṇya-vṛtti), etc.
That which has its own characteristic is a *svalakṣaṇa* (particular).
The state of being that is *svālakṣaṇya* (particularity)."
That itself is the function.
"Of the triad"; this means of intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*).
Determination (*adhyavasāya*) is the function of the intellect.
Self-conceit is the function of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and volition is that of the mind (manas).
These three— determination, self-conceit, and volition— are the respective functions of the triad.
And the fourfold function of these thirteen, beginning with the intellect (buddhi), consists of non-commonality, simultaneity, and succession.
To demonstrate its universality therein, he says: "This very [function].
This function which has been described is indeed non-universal;
the meaning is that it belongs only to that [individual] for whom it exists, and not to others as well.
That which is the manifestation of sound for the ear belongs to the ear alone,
and not to the others— the twelve [sense organs] beginning with the skin.
This should be applied in the same way everywhere.
He states the common [function]: "the common function of the instruments" (*sāmānyakaraṇavṛtti*).
It is called the common function of the instruments because it is both common and a function of the instruments.
"The five winds beginning with prāṇa.
Those winds of which prāṇa is the first are "the ones beginning with prāṇa.
These are the five winds: prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna.
In this context, *prāṇa* is that which exits through the mouth and nose;
that which is situated below the navel is *apāna*;
and that by which the fire within the body is kindled and food is digested is *samāna*.
That which, rising from the region of the navel, produces sound as it reaches the head is udāna;
that which remains pervading the entire body is vyāna.
These constitute the common function of all thirteen instruments [of perception and action]. // 29 //
Kārikā 30:
Because of the diverse powers of the vital airs (*vāyu*), he describes their simultaneous and sequential functions:
"The function of the fourfold [set] is taught as both simultaneous and sequential."
Nevertheless, whether [an object] is perceived or unperceived, the operation of the triad is preceded by that [perception].
"Simultaneously," and so forth;
"of the fourfold," however—
the word "however" (tu) is for the purpose of specification.
The simultaneous operation of this quartet—intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), mind (*manas*), and the eye—occurs within a single form.
For example, when a flash of lightning strikes in the dark and a black snake is seen, there occur simultaneously perception, determination, self-identification, and volition.
Thus, what is perceived by the eye is determined by the intellect, claimed as one's own by the ego-sense, and willed by the mind.
And regarding the phrase "and gradually for him":
the occurrence of the fourfold [doubt] in succession is intended at some time.
For one who has seen the height characteristic of both a post and a person in dim light, there arises the conceptual doubt (vikalpa): "Is it a post or a person?"
In that regard, there is the determination "it is a person" based on the contraction and extension [of the limbs];
from that, through the act of identifying with them, there arises the conceit [of "I"].
To the question of in what object this twofold operation occurs, he says: "in the seen.
To the objection that it would then not exist in the unseen, he says: "nevertheless, even in the unseen."
Likewise, even when [the object] is seen, there is a mental modification.
But [if one asks], "Is it then not of four? he says: "of three.
This means of the intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and mind (manas).
Even there, it is preceded by that; that is to say, it is preceded by the ear and so forth.
Just as for one who recollects what is to be recollected, there arise conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*), self-conceit (*abhimāna*), and determination (*adhyavasāya*).
// 30 // Now, regarding this tetrad: do these four function simultaneously, depending upon one another, each toward its own respective operation, or are they independent? To this, he says:
Each [organ] adopts its own respective mode of activity, which is caused by the mutual intentions [of the senses];
the purpose of the Puruṣa alone is the cause, for no instrument is set in motion by anything else.
"'Svāṃ svām' and so forth; [it means] their respective individual modes of livelihood."
Regarding the phrase "caused by mutual intention":
the intention of one toward another is itself the cause;
therein, the four instruments (karaṇas) engage in a function that is real and caused by mutual intention.
In that regard, having understood the underlying intent (*ākūta*) of the triad beginning with the visual consciousness (*cakṣurbuddhi*), it proceeds to illumination (*prakāśana*).

Likewise, having understood the underlying intent of the triad consisting of intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*), they proceed respectively to determination (*adhyavasāya*), self-conceit (*abhimāna*), and conceptualization (*saṅkalpana*). And these occur sequentially, being caused by their mutual underlying intents.
However, each preceding factor should be understood as being caused by the one that precedes it;
for example, when someone has heard an invitation, having perceived the activity of the sense of hearing, the intellect resolves upon going.

Having perceived its activity, the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra) thinks, "I shall eat the sweetmeats. Having perceived its activity, the mind (manas) thinks, "I shall provide plenty of ghee; why only a little?"
"He intends" [is the meaning].
In this way, even the external organs undertake their respective functions based on mutual intention.
To address whether these [elements] undertake their respective functions for their own sake or for the sake of another, he says: "The purpose of the Puruṣa alone is the cause.
The purpose of the Puruṣa consists of the enjoyment of objects and liberation (kaivalya).
That is the cause of livelihood.
Is it not the case that God is the creator of the world?
He alone created the collection of intellect and the other faculties by which the purpose of the person is accomplished.
And so it has been said:
Regarding the statement, "Impelled by God, one may go either to heaven or even into a pit," it is said in response: "The instrument is not caused to act by anyone.
The meaning is that, apart from Pradhāna, no one causes the instruments, such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth, to perform their respective functions.
If it were the agent,
why would it depend upon primordial matter (prakṛti)? Nor is primordial matter accepted by the proponent of a Lord (seśvaravādin).
If it is argued that because primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is insentient, another sentient supervisor and agent must be sought,
then the person (*puruṣa*) alone is the supervisor;
primordial matter is insentient.
This has already been stated previously.
[31] Regarding the question of how many kinds of internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) there are, he says: [Kārikā 32]
The instrument is of thirteen kinds; it performs the functions of seizing, retaining, and manifesting. And its object is tenfold.
It is to be taken away, to be maintained, and to be revealed.
"The instruments are of thirteen kinds," and so forth; namely,
the five organs of perception and the five organs of action.
And there are the three—intellect, ego, and mind.
This is the thirteenfold instrument; it is called an "instrument" (karaṇa) because it performs actions.
The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent, according to the rule: "The *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* suffixes are applied diversely."
In this regard, he explains what the function of each is, and with reference to which it is called an instrument: "It performs their seizing, retaining, and manifesting.
Thus, that instrument performs seizing and so forth;
therein, the organs of action perform seizing.
The intellect, ego, and mind constitute the faculty of retention;
the organs of perception constitute the faculty of illumination.
"What is that effect (kārya) for whose acquisition they act? To this he says: "The effect. The effect of that instrument (karaṇa) is tenfold.
Among these, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are five; and speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and sexual pleasure are five—thus it is tenfold.

The former are of two kinds: the subtle, characterized as the *tanmātras*, which are divine because their sole nature is pleasure; and the gross, such as space and the rest, which are non-divine because they consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
This is the object to be illuminated by the sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriyas*).
Because speech and the other [organs] are the agents of actions such as speaking and grasping, they constitute the "effect" (*kārya*).
In that regard, sound is [the effect] of speech;
and because that which is to be grasped is being brought forth by the two hands, both are likewise "to be brought forth" (*āhārya*).
A *vihārya* is a place for dwelling; it is called "to be brought" (*āhārya*) because it is carried by the feet through the placement of the preceding part and the stepping upon the succeeding part.
Otherwise, how could there be the joy of casting off [the body] and the joy of [receiving] bliss?
Both [the gross elements and the subtle elements] are beyond the scope of the organs of action;
they are to be held by the intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*), because they are apprehended within by their respective internal functions. // 32 //

Showing that these thirteen instruments (karaṇa) are twofold—distinguished as internal and external—the author says: The internal instrument is threefold; the external is tenfold, known as the objects of the [three internal] organs.
The external instrument pertains to the present time, while the internal instrument pertains to all three times.
"Internal organ," and so forth.
The instrument (karaṇa) is of two kinds: external and internal.
Among these, because it resides within the body, the internal organ is threefold: intellect (buddhi), ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and mind (manas).
"External [objects] are tenfold";
that is, of ten types:
the five sense organs of cognition (buddhīndriya), and...
There are five faculties of action;
their cognition arises.
"That which is external to it is called the object of the triad.
This means that the external world is designated as the "object" of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) consisting of the three [aspects],
because one penetrates the objects by means of that [internal organ].
Therefore, the object of the internal organ is twofold: the door and the object of experience.
It has been stated that while the fourfold [perception] functions with respect to the present, the threefold [perception] functions with respect to the unmanifest.
In that regard, one might ask whether there is an operation [of the senses] even toward past and future objects;
he says "no," stating: "the external belongs to the present time" (*sāmpratakālaṃ bāhyam*).
It is "time" (*kāla*) because it is measured (*kalyate*); thus, the object itself—whether past, future, or present—is what is called time.
Time does not exist apart from that [external object],
lest there be the undesirable consequence of twenty-six principles (*tattva*).
In this context, that which belongs to an external object and exists in the present— that indeed is the external.
The ear and the other [senses] manifest only present sound and so forth, not those that are past or future;
and speech and the other [organs] perform speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and experiencing pleasure only when they are present.
Not those that are past or future.
Regarding the phrase "internal with respect to the three times":
that which has three times is "three-timed" (*trikāla*).
For example, the intellect (*buddhi*) determines the present.

The same applies to the past and the future; for instance, it is said that Māndhātṛ existed and Kalkī will be king. Just as the ego conceives of the present, so too does it conceive of the past and the future.
"It was mine thus," and "it will be mine thus";
and just as the mind conceives of the present, so too does it conceive of the past and the future.
In that regard, what is this "existent" (bhūta) that one might think, "it is not mine"? What is this "future" (bhaviṣyat) that one might think, "it will not be [mine]"? // 33 // Kārikā 34:

But if coarse earth and so forth are those particulars (*viśeṣa*), then the external sense organ would perceive its own external object; in that case, earth and so forth would have to be perceived as distinct [from one another]. To this, he says:
Among those, the five organs of perception have as their objects both the specific and the non-specific;
speech has sound as its object, while the remaining [organs of action] have all five as their objects.
"the organs of cognition," and so forth.
Among those thirteen instruments, the five organs of cognition have as their objects both the specific and the non-specific.
The five objects, beginning with sound, are of two kinds: the specific (viśeṣa) and the non-specific (aviśeṣa).
Among these, those which are subtle, characterized as the mere potentials (tanmātra), are the non-specific;
those which are gross, such as earth and the rest, are the specific.
"Viśeṣāścāviśeṣāśca" is a dvandva compound.
The suffix "matup" (possessive) is applied in the sense of "those for whom these very objects exist.
Thus, the meaning is that they grasp both specific and non-specific objects.
Therein, the ear perceives gross, various, and unimpaired sounds, as well as the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*).
The nose perceives gross fragrances, such as sweet scents and the like.
And it perceives only that.
"Speech occurs":
the meaning is that its object is exclusively sound, and not any other object.
The remaining four, beginning with the hand, are the five possessors of objects (*viṣayiṇi*);
that is, they have the five objects as their domain.
In this regard, the hand grasps objects such as a jar, which possess sound, touch, form, and taste; the feet move upon the ground, which likewise possesses sound and the other qualities;
and the anus and the generative organ discharge excrement and semen, respectively, both of which possess sound and the other qualities.
By this gateway, however, all external instruments (karaṇa) should be understood as consisting solely of the five objects;
for whatever is thus dependent upon that [external instrument] is expanded, because it possesses sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
It has been stated: "The external [elements] are called the objects of the [three internal organs]. (34) How, then, are they its objects? To this he says:
Since the intellect (*buddhi*), together with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), penetrates every object,
therefore the threefold instrument is the gatekeeper,
while the remaining ones are the gates.

"With the internal organ" (*sāntaḥkaraṇā*), and so forth. Since the intellect (*buddhi*) has already been mentioned, the remaining [factors], namely the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and the mind (*manas*), constitute the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
The intellect is conjoined with these two.
"Everything": because it penetrates and grasps an object established in all three times, therefore the threefold internal organ, beginning with the intellect (*buddhi*), serves as its gate;
that is, by virtue of having gates.
The remaining organs—the organs of cognition and the organs of action—are the gates.
Through these gateways, the internal organ perceives objects.
(35) Kārikā 36:

Now, if the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) perceives every object through the medium of the external organs, what is its defining characteristic? To this he says: "These specific qualities of the [guṇas], which are like lamps, are mutually distinct."
Having illuminated the entire purpose of the person, they deliver it to the intellect.

"‘These’, etc.: the ear and so forth, speech and so forth, and the intellect and so forth—these thirteen specific qualities (guṇaviśeṣāḥ) are, in fact, the three qualities (guṇāḥ) themselves transformed through mutual subordination, bearing the designations of ‘ear’ and so on; this is the meaning. They are like lamps."
Because they illuminate their objects through their own respective functions,
they are mutually distinct;
for the function and the essential nature of one are not those of another.
If even for others than that [perceiver], the penetration of the object were established by this very [means], what would be the use of anything else?
"Entirely":

having illuminated and brought to manifestation the entire object of the person existing within the three worlds—characterized by subtle and gross objects—the eleven [faculties], beginning with the ego (ahaṅkāra), subsequently present them to the intellect (buddhi);
that is to say, they place them there.
This is the fruit of immersion (*avagāhana*).
And in that intellect (*buddhi*), which is colored by the proximity of objects, the Person (*puruṣa*) perceives.
Regarding this, it is said: "The Person [perceives] the object determined by the intellect... (SK 36).
Kārikā 37:
Now, since their status as instruments (*karaṇa*) is equal, why do the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and the others bestow [their fruits] upon the intellect (*buddhi*)?
Demonstrating that very point through its preeminence (*prādhānya*), he says:

Since it is the intellect (*buddhi*) that accomplishes every object of experience for the person (*puruṣa*), and it is that same intellect which again distinguishes the subtle difference between primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the person; [37]
"Everything," and so forth.
"With respect to each enjoyment" (*pratyupabhoga*) means for every instance of enjoyment.
Whatever enjoyment of sense objects occurs within the realms of gods, humans, and animals, he accomplishes all such sense objects belonging to the three worlds for the person.
It accomplishes [its task];
because the intellect (buddhi), being the primary factor, is nothing other than itself, therefore those instruments (karaṇas) offer their functions to the intellect.
(Just as in a village, householders pay taxes consisting of gold and other goods to the headman),
and the headman, because he stands in close proximity [to the king], is called a "lord of enjoyments" (*bhogapati*).
"And that very [intellect] distinguishes," it is said.
When the intellect is characterized by *tamas*, then it brings about everything that is presented to it;
when the intellect is dominated by *sattva*, [it acts otherwise].
Then, conjoined with knowledge, it distinguishes the difference between primary matter (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa); that is to say, it effects the separation of primary matter and the spirit,
[realizing] "primary matter is one thing, the spirit is another."
"Subtle"; because it is not an object of worldly knowledge. // 37 // It was stated that [the intellect] has as its objects both the specific and the non-specific.
Regarding this, he states what the specific and non-specific are:
"The subtle elements (tanmātras) are the non-specific; from those five, the five gross elements arise."
These are known as the specific states:
the peaceful, the terrible, and the deluded.
"‘The subtle elements’ (tanmātrāṇi), etc.:
the subtle objects are called ‘subtle elements.
Because nothing is distinguished by them, they are called ‘non-distincts’ (aviśeṣāḥ)."
Just as light situated on the tip of a minute blade of grass is not perceived and does not illuminate anything at all, so too are those [atoms] without distinction.
"From those [five], the five elements arise.
Thus, from the subtle elements (tanmātras), the five gross elements (mahābhūtas) are produced.
"These are known as the specific [elements]";
thus, from the subtle element of sound (śabda-tanmātra), space (ākāśa) arises with one quality.
In this way, from the subtle elements of touch and so forth, air and the other elements arise with two, three, four, and five qualities respectively.
And because they are distinguished by those [subtle elements],
they are called "particulars" (viśeṣas).
And as to what their nature is, he says: "They are peaceful, terrible, and delusive.
The peaceful ones bestow happiness; the terrible ones bestow suffering;
and the delusive ones bestow ignorance. (38)
Karika 39: Are there only these many specific types, or are there others as well? He says:
"The subtle [beings] and those born from mother and father..."
Together with the abundant [elements], there are three kinds of distinctions:
among them, the subtle ones are constant,
while those born of mother and father cease.
"Subtle," and so forth.
Those transmigrating beings who are subtle, characterized as mere *tanmātras*, and have become the substratum of the body, they too are "particulars" (*viśeṣas*),
because they constitute the commencement of the subtle body.
Regarding the phrase "born of mother and father":
there are six [components] born of mother and father.
Among them, hair, blood, and flesh are from the mother; sinews, bones, and marrow are from the father.
These are also specificities, because the gross body composed of the six sheaths is originated by them;
these two kinds of specificities are internal.
Regarding the term "together with the predominant" (*sahaprabhūtaiḥ*):

those external gross elements which have been described as calm, terrible, and deluded are called "predominant elements" (*prakṛṣṭabhūtāni*) by virtue of their performing the functions of providing space, expansion, cooking, moistening, and supporting for the gross body.
With these [elements], there are three specific [qualities].
"Their subtle [bodies] are fixed; those born of parents cease," it is said.
The subtle body is fixed prior to the attainment of knowledge, because it belongs to the realm of saṃsāra.
However, that which is restricted to the gross body ceases [to function], because upon each death, when it has fallen away, it culminates in the ashes of its essence. // 39 // Kārikā 40:

Regarding how this subtle body (sūkṣmaśarīra) arises, he says: The *liṅga* (the subtle body), which has arisen previously, is unattached, constant, and consists of the principles from Mahat down to the subtle elements; it migrates, devoid of enjoyment, yet permeated by latent dispositions (*bhāva*). (ISK 40)
"Produced previously," and so forth.
It is called "produced previously" because it was produced for each individual puruṣa at the initial creation by means of the Pradhāna.
He has also stated that it is unattached.
It is not obstructed anywhere;
it passes even through a mountain, having split it asunder.
'Niyatam' means constant;
that is to say, prior to the arising of knowledge.
He states what its extent is: "from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the subtle elements.
That which has the Great Principle as its beginning is "beginning with the Great"; that which has the subtle objects characterized as the tanmātras as its limit is "ending with the subtle."
The meaning is that its extent consists of this: intellect, ego-consciousness, the eleven sense organs, and the five subtle elements.
"It transmigrates" means through the three worlds.
‘Without enjoyment’ (nirupabhoga): the meaning is that, because it is devoid of the external gross body, it is incapable of the enjoyment of sense objects.
Regarding the phrase "perfumed by dispositions" (*bhāvairadhivāsitam*):
the meaning is that it is colored by factors such as mental objects (*dharma*) and so forth.
‘Liṅga’; it is so called because it undergoes dissolution (*laya*) at the time of cosmic reabsorption (*pralayakāla*). // 40 // [Commentary on Verse 41] Now, one might object:
is it not the case that only the instrument (*karaṇa*) alone transmigrates?
He asks: "What is the use of the subtle body? and answers:

"Just as a painting cannot exist without its support, and just as a shadow cannot exist without a post or other such object, so too the *liṅga* (the subtle body) does not remain without a support, being devoid of the *aviśeṣas* (the undifferentiated elements). (ISk 41)
"Variegated," and so forth:
just as a painting does not exist without a support such as a wall.
Regarding the rule "from *sthāṇu* and so forth" (*sthāṇvādibhyaḥ*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes trees, pillars, and the like.
Furthermore, there is the rule: "The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is optionally used after [words joined with] *pṛthak*, *vinā*, and *nānā*."
Thus, the ablative case also occurs;
for without them, a shadow—whether glossy or rough—does not persist.
"Similarly, without the *aviśeṣas*, the *liṅga* does not remain without a support. Here,
the *aviśeṣas* are the subtle elements (*tanmātras*),
and the *liṅga* refers to the thirteenfold instrument (*karaṇa*).
It does not persist because it lacks a support;
for by those [elements] the subtle body was initiated,
and in their absence that [body] also does not exist— thus, it lacks a support.
It does not transmigrate;
nor is a conjunction of the *puruṣa* with an instrument (*karaṇa*) possible in the absence of a substratum.
Furthermore, because the *puruṣa* is devoid of activity, it does not transmigrate either. (41)
Kārikā 42:
He explains for what purpose that very subtle body transmigrates: "This [subtle body] exists for the sake of the Puruṣa's purpose, through the connection between the cause and its effect."
Through its association with the omnipresence of primordial nature (prakṛti), the subtle body (liṅga) assumes various states like an actor.
"Caused by the purpose of the Person" (*puruṣārthahetuka*), and so forth.
The purpose of the Person has been stated to be twofold; that which has this as its cause is [the Pradhāna].
The suffix *kap* is applied as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) [to denote a collection].
"‘This’—thus has the *liṅga* (the subtle body), beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and ending with the subtle elements (*sūkṣma*), been described;
it exists like an actor.
Just as a single actor, assuming various specific roles, emerges from behind the curtain and remains present, permeated by the characters of a king, a minister, a jester, and so forth."
In the same way, the subtle body (liṅga) also, having entered various bodies, persists in the form of gods, humans, or animals.
To explain how that very [process] occurs, he says: "by means of the connection between the cause and its effect.
The cause (*nimitta*) consists of merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and so forth;
the effect (*naimittika*) consists of upward and downward movement, and so forth.
And he will say:
"In connection with those two."
To the question of whether all this arises from God or from inherent nature (svabhāva), he says: "Because of the omnipresence (vibhutva) of Prakṛti.
Prakṛti is Pradhāna; its omnipresence is its status as the creator of the universe.
Through union with that [Prakṛti], it remains present like an actor.

For the purpose of the Puruṣa must be accomplished by Prakṛti alone; thus, having produced the subtle body (liṅga) beginning with Mahat and ending with the subtle elements, she perfumes it with dharma and the other qualities.
Perfumed by those, it remains present like an actor.

It has been stated that [the world] is not produced from a Lord (īśvara), nor from inherent nature (svabhāva), but is rather "perfumed" (adhivāsita) by entities (bhāva). Regarding those [entities], he asks:
how many are there, and what do they depend upon? He says:
Innate dispositions such as virtue (dharma) and the like are natural or modified;
they are observed to reside in the instruments [the senses] or in the effects [the body], such as the embryonic stages beginning with the *kalala*.
"And those who are innate," and so forth. Those whose nature is primordial are called *sāṃsiddhika*.
And these belong only to the great sage Kapila, and not to anyone else.
For at the very moment of his arising during the initial creation, there arise simultaneously four states known as knowledge of dharma, dispassion, and sovereignty;
whereas those which arise subsequent to the initial creation for beings like us, who possess produced causes and effects through the exertion of effort,
are called "transformed" (vaikṛta).
And these are of two kinds, as it is said:
"Dharma and so forth are observed as residing in the instruments (karaṇa), while the embryo and so forth reside in the effects (kārya).
Thus, there are four [factors] beginning with Dharma.
And there are four opposites, such as non-dharma and so forth; thus, there are eight.
These function by depending upon thirteen kinds of instruments.
There are five effects.
For this [puruṣa] residing within the womb and being cast forth, there are three stages: childhood, youth, and old age;
thus, there are eight states [of existence].
It should be understood that among these, when [the puruṣa] is permeated by merit (dharma) and the other factors in the state of transformation, he transmigrates. // 43 //
It was stated [in verse 43] that [this occurs] "by way of the connection between the sign and that which is characterized by the sign.
In order to demonstrate both of these, he says:
By means of dharma there is ascent; by means of adharma there is descent;
and by means of knowledge there is liberation.
Bondage is held to arise from the opposite.
"By means of dharma," and so forth.
The signs such as dharma and the like are the causes, while the upward movement and so forth are the effects.
In this context, "upward movement by means of dharma" refers to that characterized by the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama).
The meaning is that the arrangement of gods and so forth belongs to the subtle body.
"Going downwards occurs by means of the quality of darkness (tamas)";
this refers to dwelling among the animal births. "By means of the mixed [quality]" refers to dwelling in the world of humans; such is the meaning stated.
"And by knowledge, there is liberation.

By means of the knowledge called the discernment of the difference between the primary cause (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa), the subtle body (liṅga) ceases; thereafter, the spirit becomes isolated (kevala).
"Bondage is held to arise from error";
thus, from the error of knowledge— that is, from ignorance— there is bondage to the wheel of saṃsāra, which is the repeated returning [to birth].
And that is of three kinds: the bond of nature (prakṛti-bandha),
the bond of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā-bandha),
and the bond of transformation (vikāra-bandha).
For those proponents of *prakṛti* for whom *prakṛti* alone is the supreme reality and nothing else, bondage is *prākṛtika*.

For those for whom the objects of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) consist solely of divine, semi-divine, and human enjoyments arising from sacrifices and charitable works (*iṣṭāpūrta*), [bondage is *vaikṛtika*].

For those who maintain that action is the primary factor, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) constitutes their bond; "sacrificial rites and charitable works" (*iṣṭāpūrta*) are what they call the sacrificial fee.
And so it has been said:
The Agnihotra sacrifice, austerity, truthfulness, the protection of the gods,
hospitality toward guests, and the Vaiśvadeva offering are designated as *iṣṭa*.
Lotus ponds, assembly halls, oblong ponds, temples,
the gift of food, and groves— these are designated as *pūrta* (meritorious works of public utility).

For those who maintain that the very transformation characterized by sovereignty constitutes the purpose of the Puruṣa, there is the "transformative" (vaikārika) bondage for those proponents of transformation. // 44 // Kārikā 45:
From dispassion comes dissolution into primordial nature;
from passionate attachment, there is cyclic existence.
From power comes lack of obstruction; from its opposite, the reverse occurs.

Regarding the passage beginning with "from dispassion" (*vairāgyāt*): for one who, having become detached through the observation of sense objects and so forth, remains established in the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) and does not seek after knowledge,
upon his death there occurs a dissolution (*laya*) into the eightfold *prakṛtis*— ranging from *pradhāna* down to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*)— by virtue of that dispassion.
There is a conjunction with the gross body, which serves as the means for the enjoyment of sense objects;
absorbed in that, the self considers itself as if liberated, though it is not actually liberated,
because it undergoes transmigration again at the time of creation.
But when knowledge is sought, then one is indeed liberated.
And so it has been said:
"From knowledge, from dispassion, and likewise from the complete destruction [of defilements]."
In this way liberation arises; one who is liberated is said to be established in the Self. Thus [it is said].
"Samsara arises from passionate attachment (rājasarāga). Passionate attachment is an attachment to impure objects characterized by passion; for it projects both auspicious and inauspicious karma.
Therefore, this [self] transmigrates among gods and others through the state of being born and performing sacrifices.
"From sovereignty comes non-obstruction";
thus, from the absence of sovereignty comes its opposite.
The opposite of non-obstruction is obstruction.
The meaning is that there is no attainment of those things sought; liberation, therefore, is cast far away. (45) Kārikā 46:

Among these eight forms of the intellect (*buddhi*), liberation occurs through one, while bondage and transmigration occur through seven. Regarding this sixteenfold set of causes and effects that has been mentioned, he states it briefly as fourfold:
"This is the creation of the intellect (*pratyaya-sarga*), known as error (*viparyaya*), incapacity (*aśakti*), contentment (*tuṣṭi*), and attainment (*siddhi*).
Through the mutual suppression of the inequality of the *guṇas*, its subdivisions number fifty. (ISk 46)
‘This,’ and so forth.
By the word ‘pratyaya’ (condition), the intellect (*buddhi*) is meant.
Its creation, which has been described as being of sixteen kinds, [is as follows].

This is called the "evolution of the intellect" (pratyayasarga) consisting of error (viparyaya), incapacity (aśakti), contentment (tuṣṭi), and attainment (siddhi). It is so described because these—error and the rest—are the names of this evolution of the intellect. Among these, error is ignorance (ajñāna).
Incapacity is the inability to attain knowledge even when there is a desire to learn;
contentment is the aversion toward the means to liberation;
and perfection is the attainment of knowledge.
Furthermore, there are fifty subdivisions of those four types.
To explain by what manner this occurs, he says: "by the suppression through the inequality of the qualities" (guṇavaiṣamyavimardena), and so forth.
The inequality (vaiṣamya) is the state of imbalance among sattva, rajas, and tamas, occurring through their mutual overcoming.
When one or two [of these] predominate, the other does not;
thus, through the combination of one, two, or three, there are six types of imbalance. By this, "mutual conflict" (*vimarda*) refers to the mutual agitation between two [factors].
The meaning is that it exists by reason of that.
// 46 // [Kārikā 47]— Showing those distinctions, he says:
There are five varieties of error, and incapacity arises from the deficiency of the instruments;
contentment has twenty-eight varieties, while attainment is ninefold and eightfold.
"Five varieties of error," and so forth.
There are five varieties of the creation known as ignorance (ajñāna): darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra), and blind gloom (andhatāmisra).
For this very reason, they are called afflictions (kleśas) in the Sāṃkhya-pravacana.
"Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the afflictions";
among these, ignorance is the field for the others.
"And incapacity";
this is the creation known as incapacity.
Regarding the phrase "due to the deficiency of the instruments" (*karaṇavaikalyāt*):
the instruments are both external and internal.
By changing the case ending, it should be construed as follows: that incapacity which possesses twenty-eight varieties [arises] from the deficiency of those two.
And the impairment of the instruments occurs through the suppression caused by the disharmony of the qualities.
"Contentment is ninefold and attainment is eightfold";
this means that the creation of contentment is of nine types,
while the creation of attainment is of eight types.
Taken together, these constitute fifty varieties. [47] Showing them along with their internal subdivisions, he says: [Kārikā 48]
The division of darkness (tamas) is eightfold, that of delusion (moha) is likewise;
great delusion (mahāmoha) is tenfold,
and gloom (tāmisra) is eighteenfold.
In that way, there is the Andhatāmisra hell.
"Distinction is of darkness," and so forth. "Darkness" (tamas) refers to ignorance (avidyā); it is the ground for the production of the subsequent [qualities].
And that is the primordial nature (prakṛti);
for those who know the truth, there is no liberation even when detachment exists,
because of the absence of knowledge.
Consequently, their dissolution occurs into those very eight primal natures; thus, ignorance is eightfold, because its objects are eightfold.
The phrase "of delusion" (mohasya) implies that its eightfold division follows from the word "and" (ca).
Delusion (moha) is what is meant here by the term "ignorance" (asmitā).
Even the gods are subject to destruction.
Relying upon the eightfold sovereignty, they consider themselves imperishable;
consequently, they possess an eightfold delusion,
because sovereignty is eightfold.
"Tenfold is great delusion (*mahāmoha*).
Thus, attachment (*rāga*), which is the underlying tendency toward pleasure (*sukhānuśaya*), is called "great delusion.
And that, occurring with respect to divine and non-divine objects, becomes tenfold.
Among these, five are subtle, characterized as the *tanmātras*,
and are twofold because their sole nature is pleasure;
five are gross, such as earth and the rest.
They are non-divine because they consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

"Tāmisra is eighteenfold. The latent tendency toward suffering, which is hatred, is called tāmisra. It is eighteenfold because it manifests with respect to the eightfold sovereign powers and the ten kinds of objects.
"Thus there is Andhatāmisra.
The meaning is that just as Tāmisra is eighteenfold, so too is this [Andhatāmisra].
The fear of death is called Andhatāmisra.
And that [power] manifests with respect to the eightfold sovereignty and the tenfold objects; thus, it is of eighteen kinds.
"Likewise, there is blind darkness (andhatāmisra). The meaning is that just as *tāmisra* is eighteenfold, so too is this.
The fear of death is called *andhatāmisra*.
And that [ignorance] exists only with respect to the eightfold sovereign powers (*aṣṭaguṇaiśvarya*) and the tenfold objects (*daśavidha-viṣaya*).
Thus, ignorance is said to have sixty-two divisions. // 48 // *Kārikā 49*
It has been stated that incapacity results from the impairment of the instruments; in order to show its various divisions, he says:
"Incapacity is taught as the destruction of the eleven organs together with the destruction of the intellect."
And there are seventeen kinds of errors regarding the intellect, namely those concerning contentment and accomplishment.
"Eleven," and so forth.
There are exactly eleven impairments of the eleven sense faculties:
deafness, blindness, and loss of smell for the ears, eyes, and nose, respectively; [and so on for the remaining senses].
Deafness of speech, numbness of the tongue,
and madness of the mind.
The deficiencies of the hands, feet, and genitals are lameness, crippledness, and impotence; of the sense of touch, leprosy; and of the anus, upward movement of wind (udāvarta).
Deafness, blindness, loss of smell, muteness, as well as dullness of intellect,
insanity, leprosy, skin diseases, impotence, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and lameness— thus [it is said].
Therefore, the impairment of the faculties has been taught by the Sāṃkhya teachers as incapacity.
Regarding the phrase "along with the destructions of the intellect" (*saha buddhivadhaiḥ*):
the destructions of the intellect are taught to be its incapacity.
To the question "How many are they?", he says: "The means of knowledge for contentments and accomplishments are seventeenfold.
There are nine contentments and eight accomplishments.
The seventeen types of defects of the intellect (*buddhi*) which are the opposites of the [qualities of] water to be described hereafter should be understood.
Thus, incapacity (*aśakti*) has twenty-eight divisions, by which one becomes incapable of action in due order.
Now, it was stated that this is the "creation of the intellect" (*pratyayasarga*);
however, one might object that this impairment of the senses is not the creation of the intellect, but rather a certain creation of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*). This is true;
nevertheless, because egoism is itself a creation of the intellect, its creation is also called the "creation of the intellect."
Or, dharma is the causal condition for creation. // 49 // [The author] states the different types of contentment (tuṣṭi): [Kārikā 50]...
There are four internal [contentments] known as those consisting of nature, material resources, time, and fortune;
and five external ones arising from the cessation of objects.
Thus, nine contentments are recognized.
By the words "internal" (*ādhyātmikāḥ*) and so forth:
those satisfactions (*tuṣṭi*) whose names are "nature" (*prakṛti*) and so on are described as such.
In this context, "nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to the primary cause (*pradhāna*).

He who is satisfied by the mere instruction that "this very [Prakṛti], having transformed itself through the manifest form, effects bondage and liberation," for him there is the satisfaction called "Ambhas" (the Water), which is named after Prakṛti.
That by which liberation is grasped or attained is called "appropriation" (*upādāna*);
here, this refers to the insignia of renunciation, such as the staff and so forth.
Liberation is not achieved through innate knowledge alone.

From this second instruction, "and by means of grasping," he becomes fully satisfied that liberation is to be attained right here; thus, for this renunciant, his second satisfaction called "grasping" is termed "water."
They are called *kālā* (time) because they depend on time (*kalayati*).

Since liberation does not occur in this very life merely through the material cause of *prakṛti* while one is transmigrating by means of another sign— the subtle elements beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*)—
the contentment of one who remains waiting for time based on this third teaching is called the obstruction known as *kālā*-contentment.
Liberation belongs to one who possesses further fortune;
it does not come through nature, material causes, or time alone.
Since there is someone whose lot is adverse, he who remains satisfied with this fourth instruction and relies upon fortune is said to have the "fourth rain."
These four are called "internal" because they pertain to the self, considering that it is by means of the self that one must be liberated.

And because of the cessation of external objects; this "cessation" (uparama), which is the turning away from sound and the other sense-objects, occurs in five ways through the perception of the defects in acquisition, preservation, loss, attachment, and injury.

In that regard, there is great suffering in the acquisition of objects; this is the fifth contentment, called *sutāra*, which belongs to one who has desisted from acquisition upon seeing its defects because those objects are so few.

Objects of sense can be acquired, but their protection is difficult and would be attended by much suffering arising from many [causes]; therefore, this sixth contentment, which belongs to one who has desisted from observing the need for protection, is called "Supāra" (the Excellent Crossing).
Objects of the senses can be acquired, protected, and provided for when they perish;

however, while being enjoyed, they produce great attachment to the self, and their non-attainment causes great suffering. Because one perceives these faults of association (*saṅga*), one becomes indifferent toward them; this eighth contentment is called "the unsurpassed water."
Everything is possible; however, enjoyment is not possible without harming living beings.
Since great misfortune results from the injury of living beings, this contentment of one who has desisted through seeing the fault in violence is called the ninth, *uttamāmbhas*.
These five are called "external" because they occur by way of the objects of the senses.
And those internal [attainments] are preceded by that,
because for one who is intent upon external objects, internal contentment is impossible.

In this regard, although it has been taught that nature (*prakṛti*), material cause (*upādāna*), and time (*kāla*) are not means to liberation, for one who does not accept this due to aversion, there are nine contentments (*tuṣṭi*): four internal and five external arising from the cessation of sense-objects.
These are called the "injuries to the intellect" (*buddhi-vadha*).
The power of those [sixty-four arts] is included within them.
Among those sixty-four, the names beginning with "Great" (*mahat*) are applied by way of inversion.
Both of these are also included within the intellect (*buddhi*), because they are its emanations. // 50 //
Kārikā 51:
Regarding how many types there are of the attainment characterized by knowledge and ignorance, he says:
reasoning, oral instruction, study, the three suppressions of suffering, and the acquisition of a friend.
Generosity and the eight accomplishments; prior to accomplishment, the threefold goad.
"Reasoning, oral instruction, and study," and so forth.
Accomplishment (*siddhi*) is the attainment of knowledge; its varieties arise from the variety of means.
Regarding "ūha":

for one whose intellect is refined by impressions from previous births, as he contemplates the cause of bondage and liberation, there arises in him the knowledge of the distinction between *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*. His first attainment, which has reasoning (*ūha*) as its cause, is called *tāra*. This refers to one in whom the knowledge of reality arises upon hearing the recitation of the Sāṃkhya treatise belonging to another.
That accomplishment, which has sound as its cause, is called the second, Sutāra.

For one in whom knowledge arises after having studied the Sāṃkhya treatise— both in its words and its meaning— through the relationship of disciple and teacher, [that knowledge] has study as its cause;
for it is through study that it is fully understood.
This is called the third, Tāravi.
"Three [types of knowledge] are for the destruction of suffering. Thus, whoever is afflicted by internal, external, or celestial suffering will seek knowledge for the sake of its destruction—
whether through reasoning, verbal instruction, or study.
For him, there are three [accomplishments] called *pramāda*, *pramudita*, and *modana*, which have that [obstruction] as their cause,
because the means are threefold.
It should be understood that the first three accomplishments do not have suffering as their cause.
"Attaining a friend":
this refers to one who, having realized the truth, attains knowledge by relying on a friend;
for such a person, [the attainment of knowledge] is preceded by the attainment of a friend.
For a friend, out of affection, illuminates knowledge;
this is called the seventh [bhūmi], Ramyakā.
Generosity is the cause of accomplishment;
for when the Knower is propitiated by generosity, he bestows knowledge.
This is called the eighth [stage], "Always Joyful."
The opposites of these are the non-attainments (*asiddhi*).
When one does not infer due to dullness of intellect, that is non-attainment caused by lack of inference (*anūha*).
When one, though capable and even hearing the Sāṃkhya treatise, does not understand it due to weakness of intellect, that is non-attainment caused by the word (*śabda*).
This is indeed a defect of the intellect (*buddhidoṣa*).
For one who does not study under a teacher due to a defect of the intellect, there is non-attainment caused by that lack of study.
Where there is no gathering of friends and no giving—these eight types of non-attainment, which are slayers of the intellect, are included within incapacity (*aśakti*).
And for those non-establishments, there are designations such as "deception," "fever," "delusion," and so forth;
they are included within the category of cognition because they are of the nature of mental construction.
"Prior to perfection, the goad is threefold.
This means that prior to that eightfold perfection, that which was described as threefold—namely, error, incapacity, and contentment—is called a "goad" because it is like a goad.
For by this, the world is rendered powerless and remains bound within the wheel of saṃsāra.
In this context, because it is stated that "bondage is held to be the result of error and so forth," the fivefold ignorance is the hook (*aṅkuśa*).
Incapacity is the deficiency of the instruments; for from that results the non-attainment of knowledge, and thus it is a hook.
Contentment is also a goad.

At that time, because one is satisfied with the mere instruction that "nature, material cause, time, and fortune are the means to liberation" and that "one is liberated through the cessation of sense-objects," one will not seek after knowledge.
But when he seeks [the truth], then he is "without restraint"— this is the meaning.
These are the fifty categories consisting of the various divisions of the creation of the objective world (pratyayasarga), as well as the ten [qualities] beginning with existence (astitva).
And these have been specified within this very group of seventy. Thus the compiler said:
"Existence, unity, purposefulness, subservience to another, distinctness, and the absence of an agent."
Union, separation, the plurality of souls, the stability of the body, and the remaining mode of existence. Thus [ends the section].
"Unity, purposiveness, and subservience to another" are stated with reference to the Pradhāna;
"distinctness, non-agency, and multiplicity" with reference to the Puruṣa;
and "existence, conjunction, and disjunction" with reference to both.
Stability (sthiti) refers to the fundamental subtle [nature];
as he will say: "It persists by the power of the formative forces (saṃskāra).
These are the sixty categories (padārtha).
For that purpose, the treatise is called the *Ṣaṣṭitantra*.
(51) It has been stated that the previously arisen *liṅga* (the subtle body), permeated by the *bhāvas* (dispositions), transmigrates. (Kārikā 52)
In this regard, as to whether entities also arise first or whether it is only the mark [that arises], he says:
there is no mark without entities, nor is there the accomplishment of entities without a mark.
From that, the two-fold creation proceeds: that which is called the Linga and that which is called Bhava.
"‘Not without,’ and so forth:
if entities have not arisen previously, then without them, even the characteristic (liṅga) does not exist;
for the characteristic exists for the sake of wandering in saṃsāra, and entities are the cause of saṃsāra."
"Without a mark (liṅga), there is no accomplishment of existence";
that is, without a mark, there is no non-accomplishment of existence, because existents are dependent upon marks.
Since this is so, therefore creation (sarga) is of two kinds—called *liṅga* and called *bhāva*—because of its predominance; it is called *sarga* because it is created (*sṛjyate*). // 52 // Kārikā 53:

Showing that the creation of the elements (bhūtasarga) is just as these two [the subtle body and the organs] were previously produced, he says: "The divine consists of eight varieties, the animal is fivefold,
and the human is of one kind."
In brief, creation is composed of the elements.
"Consisting of eightfold conceptualization," and so forth.
This belongs to the gods, thus it is "divine" (*daiva*).
It is of eight kinds.
Namely: the Brāhma, the Prājāpatya,
and the Saura.
The Asura, the Gandharva, and the Yakṣa.
The Rākṣasa and the Paiśāca.

"And that pertaining to the animal kingdom is fivefold. This [rebirth] belongs to those born as animals; it is of five kinds due to the divisions of domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and immobile beings.
Among these, those beginning with cattle and ending with donkeys are domestic animals (*paśu*);
those beginning with lions and ending with cats are wild beasts (*mṛga*);
and those beginning with swans and ending with mosquitoes are birds (*pakṣin*).
Those beginning with serpents and ending with worms are the crawling creatures (sarīsṛpa);
those beginning with trees and ending with pillars are the stationary beings (sthāvara).
"And human [form] is of one kind.
This belongs to humans (mānuṣya);
it is so called because such a configuration is of a single type.
Even the division into Brahma and so forth arises from the conceptualization of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, serving as the cause for the conventional usage of time.
"Samāsataḥ" means in brief;
[as for] "vistaraṃ," it refers to its detailed [explanation].
The four divisions known as viviparous (jarāyuja), oviparous (aṇḍaja), sweat-born (uṣmaja), and soil-born (udbhijja) should be seen in other treatises;
the soil-born are the stationary beings (sthāvara).
"Elemental creation" (*bhautikaḥ sargaḥ*): that which arises from the elements (*bhūteṣu*) is elemental;
the meaning is the production of the world.

And that [aggregate] is of two kinds. (53) Showing that within the gross body, one or another [element] exists in some cases with predominance, he says: *The Verse 53:* [The commentary: ...and that [aggregate] is of two kinds. (53) Showing that within the gross body, one or another [element] exists in some cases with predominance, he says:—
The creation is vast in *sattva* at the top, vast in *tamas* at its root,
and vast in *rajas* in the middle;
it extends from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
"Upwards," and so forth. That creation of which Brahmā is the beginning and the "stamba" (the trunk) extends down to the grass and shrubs—
that is the creation from Brahmā down to the stamba.
That is "upward" and "abounding in *sattva*. Because the world of the gods (*devaloka*) is superior, it is "upward"; the meaning is that one is characterized by *sattva* there.
This is because the world of the gods is abundant in *sattva*.
"And the creation rooted in darkness is vast";
thus, the animal realm is the root, because of its inferiority.
At that root, darkness is predominant because of the abundance of the quality of tamas.
"In the middle, it is vast with dust.
This means in the middle of the world of humans (*manuṣyaloka*). Because of the state of being higher and lower [relative to one another], there is an abundance of suffering therein. // 54 //
Kārikā 55:
If it is the *liṅga* that transmigrates through the three worlds,
then it is that very thing which experiences worldly pleasure or pain.
Because that very [liṅga] is characterized by worldly existence, he says:
"In that regard, the conscious person (puruṣa) undergoes the suffering caused by old age and death;
therefore, as long as the liṅga has not ceased, suffering exists by its very nature. (ISk 55)
Regarding the phrase "In that regard" and so forth:
"caused by aging and death" in those worlds is intended as an illustration of the four types of suffering.
[The first is] the suffering of the womb.
The suffering of birth,
the suffering of old age, and the suffering of death.
In that regard, the suffering of contraction and expansion for one who has entered as if into blinding darkness within the mother’s womb is the suffering of the embryo.
The suffering of birth is the pain of one being born, emerging from the mother’s belly.
The suffering of old age is the pain of stumbling over thresholds, thorns, and so forth.
The suffering of death belongs to one who abandons the gross body at the time of death.

This is included within the category of internal suffering (ādhyātmika-duḥkha) as the suffering of dissatisfaction; the Puruṣa experiences it because he is conscious, whereas the subtle body (liṅga) does not, because it is insentient—this is the intended meaning.
He states for how long [this lasts]: "until the cessation of the liṅga.
The meaning is: as long as the liṅga has not ceased.
And its cessation results from the knowledge of the distinction between Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
And because it is thus, therefore suffering exists by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*).
The meaning is that in the states of the embryo, the fetus, and so forth, there is suffering by way of its own nature.
Even though one may attain pleasure within the three worlds, [it is nonetheless suffering].
That was not mentioned because it is not constant;
however, the suffering of old age and so forth is constant. // 55 // Kārikā 56:
Is this creation of entities, marks, and their manifestation from Īśvara,
as it is said:
"Impelled by Īśvara, one may go either to heaven or even to hell"?
Thus, or rather, [is it] from the Person (puruṣa),
as it is said:
"The Person alone is all this, whatever has been and whatever is to be."
Or is it from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), as it is said:
"This entire world is indeed of the nature of intrinsic nature; for the winds and so forth are not created by anyone."
Regarding this, he says:
"Thus, this undertaking—beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the specific gross elements—is brought about by Nature (prakṛti);
for the sake of the liberation of each individual Puruṣa, it is an undertaking for the sake of another, as if it were for its own sake. (ISk 56)
‘Thus this is produced by primordial nature’ (prakṛtikṛta), and so forth.
‘Begun’ (ārambha) means that which is commenced.
‘Produced by primordial nature’ (prakṛtikṛta) means produced by the primary cause (pradhāna).
The meaning is that it was not created by Īśvara or others.
The three worlds consist of the three *guṇas*, and they arise from *prakṛti* itself, which is composed of the three *guṇas*.
It is not innate,
because that would entail the presence of contrary qualities and defects, and because it would involve a lack of restriction regarding location.
He states what its nature is: "beginning with the Great One (mahat) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣabhūta).
Intellect (buddhi) is the beginning of this [evolutionary] process;
and the elements are those in the three worlds which, having undifferentiated forms, are called the gross body (sthūlaśarīra).
And as for objects:
external objects are both subtle and gross;
that which has these at its limit or conclusion is described as such.
By this, the three [topics] known as existence (bhāva), the mark (liṅga), and creation (sarga) have been explained.
To the question "For what purpose is this commencement of Pradhāna?", he says: "For the sake of the liberation of each individual Puruṣa.
The commencement is for the sake of the liberation of every single Puruṣa, because Puruṣas are many.
He shows that [the creation] is manifold, both in the creation of dispositions (*bhāva*) and in the creation of elements (*bhūta*).
For it should be understood that this undertaking is for the sake of liberation and for the sake of the enjoyment of objects;
indeed, the purpose of the Person (*puruṣārtha*) must be accomplished by means of Pradhāna.
And that [activity] is of two kinds:
the enjoyment of objects and isolation. Having accomplished both of these, it ceases.
"'For its own sake' (svārthaḥ): the meaning is that just as Devadatta acts for his own sake alone and does not perform penance for another, so too does the Pradhāna. // 56 //
[Objection: But surely, activity preceded by intelligence belongs only to that which possesses consciousness.
Since the *pradhāna* is insentient, how could it—having first joined the *puruṣa* with objects throughout the three worlds and then having released him through meditation—cease its activity?
How can there be such activity?
This is not a fixed rule, for activity is observed even among insentient things in the world. As it has been said:
Just as the flow of milk from the insentient [cow] occurs for the sake of the growth of the calf,
so does the activity of the Pradhāna occur for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa.
"‘For the sake of the calf’s growth’ and so forth:
the growth of the calf is its nourishment;
[the milk] is the cause of that."
"Just as the manifestation of milk occurs from that which is insentient";
[this refers to] the insentient.
For example, grass and so forth, which are insentient, when eaten and drunk by a cow, [produce milk].
Thinking, "The calf must be nourished," [the milk] transforms itself into the form of milk and, having accomplished its purpose, ceases to exist. // 57 // Kārikā 58:

If the activity of Pradhāna is for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa, then since isolation (kaivalya) of the Puruṣa was already established prior to that activity, what is the purpose of that activity?
And so they have said: "If someone setting out for the sake of honey should find honey near a village, why would he go to the mountain? Thus it is said.
To this, it is said:
Just as the world engages in activities for the sake of satisfying its desires, so too does the Unmanifest engage for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa. (ISk 58)
"‘Autsukyam’ (longing),” and so forth.

Just as people engage in desired activities for the sake of satisfying a longing, in the same way, during the state of dissolution (*pralaya*), the *puruṣa* also causes the *pradhāna* to act in order to satisfy that longing which exists for the sake of liberation (*mokṣa*). // 58 //
Karika 59: He states another example:
"Just as a dancer, having displayed her performance to the audience, desists from dancing."
In the same way, having manifested herself to the Puruṣa, Prakṛti desists.
"Of the stage," and so forth.
She who dances is a dancer (*nartakī*). Having thus displayed her dance for the stage, she turns away from that dance; she desists.

Having seen "I have been seen by him," and thus having fulfilled her purpose, Prakṛti—meaning the Pradhāna—having fully revealed herself to the Puruṣa in the form of various states such as gods and so forth, departs and ceases to act. // 59 // Kārikā 60: [The following: "The union of the two, which is the cause of the world's production, occurs through the qualities of the one and the distinctness of the other. [This is the first half of verse 60.]
But surely, an actress achieves her own purpose from the stage, whereas the purpose of the Person (puruṣārtha) is the Prakṛti’s own purpose, by which she acts in this way? To this he says:
"By various means, the benefactress [acts] for the sake of the Person who does not benefit her."
Though he himself is devoid of virtue, he acts fruitlessly for the sake of that virtuous person.
"By various means," and so forth.
Previously, by means of the seven methods beginning with virtue (dharma), she benefits [the soul] by manifesting herself within the three spheres;
immediately thereafter, by means of the single method called knowledge (jñāna), she becomes beneficial by bringing about isolation (kaivalya).
Regarding the phrase "toward a man who does no harm":
the man does not reciprocate that [benefit] by thinking, "I have been helped by her."
Furthermore, it assists that [consciousness].
He says that this is not so: "Because it possesses qualities while [the other] is devoid of qualities.
Since it possesses qualities, primordial nature (prakṛti) is active.

"Because it is devoid of qualities, the Puruṣa is inactive. He pursues its purpose, which is twofold: the enjoyment of objects and liberation. This purpose of that Puruṣa is of two kinds—the enjoyment of sense-objects and absolute isolation (kaivalya).
He renders that useless,
because there is an absence of purpose for it in its manifested form.
It reveals itself, but not in its unmanifest form.
(60) For instance: the state of equilibrium of the *guṇas* is *prakṛti*.
And for what reason does it not manifest itself in its entirety, and why does the person (puruṣa) also not perceive it in every respect?
And so they have said:
"The supreme form of the qualities does not come within the range of vision;
that which has reached the range of vision is a mere illusory thing, void. To this, he says:
"It is my conviction that nothing exists more delicate than Prakṛti;
once she has been seen by the Puruṣa, thinking 'I have been seen,' she does not present herself for sight again."
"From primordial nature" (*prakṛteḥ*), and so forth.
"More delicate" (*sukumārataram*) means more subtle than the other.
This is what is meant: [the intellect] manifests [objects] previously in a manifest form, but not even in an unmanifest form.
By which, in the state of knowledge, the intellect becomes [realized] as my own nature: "There is nothing else more subtle than this which remains to be seen by the Puruṣa."
"Since I have been seen," thinking thus, that nature (prakṛti), having been seen by him in its manifested form, does not undergo further perception by the puruṣa.
Because there is no object to be seen.
And thus, in this way, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) manifests itself in every respect, and the person (*puruṣa*) perceives it in every respect. // 61 //
Therefore, there is neither bondage for the Puruṣa, nor transmigration, nor liberation; thus it is said:
"Therefore, truly no one is bound, nor is anyone liberated, nor does anyone transmigrate."
It is primordial nature (prakṛti), depending on various substrates, that transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated.
"Therefore, he is not bound," and so forth.
Because there is an absence of bondage, he is not bound.
Furthermore, since the *puruṣa* is not something produced, there is no bondage for him.
He is not liberated from that bondage,
nor does he transmigrate because of his lack of activity;
"someone" means a person (puruṣa).
To the question, "To whom, then, do bondage and so forth belong? he says: "Prakṛti transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated.

But [one might object]: "Since she is delicate, bondage and so forth are simply not possible for her. To this he replies: "She is cast into various substrata. In this context, the substrata are the creations consisting of the states of existence (bhāva) and the genders (liṅga).
They are of various kinds, like the *prakṛti* and the *puruṣa*. (62) And therefore, demonstrating that they indeed have diverse substrata, he says: [Kārikā 63]
Prakṛti binds herself to herself by means of the seven forms alone; and she herself, by means of a single form, liberates her for the sake of the Puruṣa's purpose.
"By means of forms," and so forth.
Form (*rūpa*) and the other [aggregates] are stated to be the forms of the Buddha.
"By seven."
Having abandoned knowledge, they become one with nature (prakṛti).

That very nature, by means of the self itself, binds the self for the sake of the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha) through the subtle body (liṅga), which consists of the principles from the Great One (mahat) down to the subtle elements. And this bondage is threefold.
And that *liṅga* transmigrates only toward an object perfumed by dispositions (*bhāva*) and so forth;
thus, it is *prakṛti* alone that transmigrates.
"And that very [nature]," it is said; nature liberates itself for the sake of the person's purpose, which is isolation (kaivalya).
Regarding the term "ekarūpeṇa" (in a single form): it means that which is both one and its own form; the sense is "by way of the form called cognition."
The meaning is that it withdraws its unmanifest self with respect to that person toward whom it produces cognition;
for qualities such as merit (dharma) and so forth are not properties of the Puruṣa, nor is it bound by them,
nor does it transmigrate.
Because it lacks the nature of a sign;
nor is it liberated, because it is itself bondage. // 63 //
Kārikā 64:
Thus, he explains how that very knowledge arises by which one is liberated:
"In this way, through the practice of reality, [the realization arises] without remainder: 'I am not, nothing is mine, there is no I.'"
From the absence of error, pure and absolute knowledge arises.
"Thus, from the practice of the principles," and so forth.
The word "thus" (evam) is to be connected with what is about to be said.
The principles (tattva) are twenty-five.
Furthermore, *abhyāsa* (practice) is the repeated cultivation of their true nature.
[This means: "I do not exist within this subtle body and the elemental body; rather, I am *prakṛti* (primordial nature)."
‘Not mine,’ and so forth;
this is not mine, but rather belongs to primordial nature (prakṛti).

"Neither am I [the body]," nor "I am not Prakṛti"— through such practice of reality (tattva-abhyāsa), knowledge arises from that which is non-erroneous, free from the conceit of "I," and devoid of doubt.
He says it is "of such a kind" by stating: "without remainder.
This means it is complete and pure, being solitary and unique due to the departure of the impurities of saṃsāra. // 64 // Kārikā 65:

Now, to the question "What does the person (puruṣa) see by means of knowledge?", he says: By that [knowledge], the person, established like a spectator and remaining in its own nature, beholds Prakṛti, whose productivity has ceased due to the fulfillment of her purpose, and who has withdrawn from her seven forms. (ISk 65)
"By that," and so forth.
