That primordial nature (*prakṛti*) with respect to which the knowledge of the original state arises is described as such because its procreative activity—characterized by the manifestation known as creation—is ceased.
Alternatively, it is by virtue of that object from which one turns away from sense objects due to the cessation of procreation.
Nature (prakṛti) becomes withdrawn from the seven forms, beginning with the mental faculty (dharma);
the meaning is that even its association with the objective world ceases for it.
The Puruṣa perceives nature in such a state, which is unmanifest in form.
"He stands like a spectator" means that just as a spectator watches a dancer who has both commenced and concluded her dance,
so too does the Puruṣa observe the creation that has both been set in motion and brought to an end.
‘Established in oneself’ (svasthaḥ) means established in the Self (ātman), not established in primordial nature (prakṛti),
because he has withdrawn from nature. // 65 //
Kārikā 66:

Now, if Nature (*prakṛti*), having ceased its productivity with respect to the Spirit (*puruṣa*)—and since that Nature is omnipresent and thus still possesses conjunction at that time—why does the body not arise again? To this, he says:
Thinking "I have seen [her]," the one remains indifferent; thinking "I have been seen," the other ceases.
Even though their union occurs, there is no further purpose for creation.
"I have seen [them]," and so forth.
Of those two, one person is indifferent, because he is entirely... [detached].
Just as a spectator disregards an actress because his desire for her has ceased.
"I have been seen; thus another has ceased. Another nature has ceased, meaning its productive activity has stopped, thinking, "In every way, I have been seen by him."
Furthermore, even when those two are in conjunction, there is no purpose for creation;
for creation exists for the sake of experiencing objects. Since its purpose has been fulfilled in that very state, it does not initiate creation again.
For a dancer does not begin her dance again on the stage once she has been rendered indifferent by the spectators.
If liberation is attained through the knowledge of the Self, [then...]
To the question, "Why does the body not cease immediately thereafter?", he says:
"Upon the attainment of perfect knowledge, when dharma and the other [factors] no longer serve as causes,
[the body] persists by the force of the *saṃskāras*."
Holding his body like the whirling of a wheel.
"From the attainment of right knowledge," and so forth.
Right knowledge is the knowledge of the Self (ātman).
The meaning is: from its attainment, that is, from the acquisition of the knowledge of the Self.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of the non-attainment of the cause for dharmas and so forth": "non-cause" (akāraṇa) means that which is not a cause;
it is precisely in the case of such non-attainment of a cause that this has been stated.
Because, through the attainment of right knowledge, those factors such as the dharmas become powerless, like seeds burnt by fire.
By the force of impressions (*saṃskāra*) from a previous birth, the person remains having assumed a body.

How so? Like the whirling of a potter’s wheel. Just as the whirling of a wheel continues for some time due to momentum even after the potter’s activity has ceased, so too does the body [persist]; this is the meaning. // 67 //
Regarding the question of when liberation occurs:
it happens upon the dissolution of the body, because the purpose has been fulfilled and the primary cause (pradhāna) has ceased its activity.
One attains both the certain and the absolute state of absolute liberation.
"Upon the dissolution of the body," and so forth;
the meaning is that when the subtle (liṅga) and elemental (bhautika) bodies have become separate, they go to their dissolution within those [elements] as they were originally produced.
"Because its purpose has been fulfilled, the Pradhāna ceases [its activity].
Thus, the Pradhāna, having transformed itself into the form of the Liṅga, desists;
upon this cessation, both attain isolation (kaivalya).
"Both certain and final.
In this context, "certain" means that liberation (*kaivalya*) necessarily occurs through the arising of the knowledge of the Self.
"Final" means that even though the conjunction of those two [the Self and Nature] still exists, there is no further creation because there is no longer any purpose for it. // 68 //
Kārikā 69. Showing purity in the seventy [verses], he says:
This secret knowledge of the human goal has been fully proclaimed by the Supreme Sage.
It is therein that the persistence, arising, and dissolution of all beings are contemplated.
"Knowledge of the goal of man," and so forth.
Knowledge that has the goal of man as its object is "knowledge of the goal of man.
This knowledge of the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) is the primary [purpose].
This is because liberation, the goal of human endeavor, is attained by means of this.
This is a secret that must not be disclosed;
the meaning is that it should not be given to anyone other than virtuous people.
"Proclaimed by the supreme seer" means revealed by the sage Kapila.
"Wherein the stability, origination, and dissolution of beings are considered.
In that knowledge, the stability and other states of beings—from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—are established.
Among these, "stability" (sthiti) is the continuous persistence of those things that have arisen.

And that [evolution] occurs in three locations— among gods, humans, and animals— from the primary matter (pradhāna) as it is projected, up to the five great elements from the subtle elements (tanmātra).
At the withdrawal of creation, there is the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), wherein everything likewise proceeds by way of reverse order.
For example, earth and the other elements dissolve into their respective subtle essences (*tanmātra*), continuing up to the Primal Nature (*pradhāna*).
By this, it is stated that there exists nothing apart from the twenty-five principles (*tattva*). // 69 // *Kārikā* 70:
How is it known that this was taught by the Sage? To this he says:
"This purifying and supreme [teaching] the Sage gave to Āsuri out of compassion;
Āsuri, in turn, gave it to Pañcaśikha."
And by him, the Tantra was composed in many ways.
"‘This’; and so forth.
‘Pure’;
that is to say, because it purifies these three types of suffering."
It is called "foremost" because it exists prior to all divisions.
"The Sage gave [this] to Āsuri out of compassion.
Thus, for the great sage Kapila, four qualities beginning with Dharma were born simultaneously.
Among these, compassion arose in the Sage when he beheld the world abiding in blinding darkness through the state known as ignorance.

Urged by her, he went to Āsuri, a Brāhmaṇa of his own lineage who was one thousand years old, and said to him: "Āsuri, do you take delight in the duties of a householder? He replied to him: "Venerable sir, I do not take delight."
Again, when a thousand years were complete, he went to him and spoke in the same manner;
he too replied, "O Blessed One, I do not find delight. Then the sage said, "If you are dispassionate..."
"Come, practice the holy life"— thus he was addressed;
having accepted this, he abandoned the duties of a householder and went forth into homelessness.
Out of compassion for that disciple, he gave it to him in brief:
"Verily, this was darkness alone"; in that darkness, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) was indeed the first.
Tamas is predominant;
he is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Puruṣa.
Āsuri, out of compassion, also gave that very same [teaching] in summary form to his own disciple Pañcaśikha.
"By him"—that is, by the sage Pañcaśikha—the tantra was composed in many ways;
it was made into sixty sections, known as the *Ṣaṣṭitantra*.
For it is therein that the sixty topics are explained. // 70 //
[Objection: "But let there be only the *Ṣaṣṭitantra*; what is the purpose of [this work] consisting of seventy [verses]? To this, he states the purpose for composing his own treatise:
"Through the lineage of disciples..."
"This has been set forth in Āryā verses by Īśvarakṛṣṇa,
who, possessing noble intelligence, has correctly understood the established doctrine and summarized it."
"By a lineage of disciples," and so forth:
from the Sage Āsuri came Pañcaśikha, as well as Garga, Gautama, and others down to the wandering mendicant named Īśvarakṛṣṇa— by this lineage of disciples.
Thus, having correctly understood the *Ṣaṣṭitantra*— the established doctrine (siddhānta) that has come down in the form of knowledge,
which is the concise *Ṣaṣṭitantra* meaning the knowledge known as the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśatitattva*).
Āryamati: one who possesses noble intelligence by virtue of having realized the knowledge of reality.
"By the noble ones" means by seventy [verses].
"Due to the assault of the threefold suffering."
"This is the purifier";
thus it was declared by seventy [verses]. // 71 // Kārikā 72:
Regarding this, he says that many topics exist in the *Ṣaṣṭitantra* which have not been stated here:
"The topics that are indeed in the *Saptati* are the topics of the entire *Ṣaṣṭitantra*."
They are devoid of narratives and also free from the arguments of opponents.

The passage beginning with "in the seventy" and continuing with the text starting from "This is the creation of the cognitive faculties, known as error, incapacity, contentment, and attainment," refers to all that has been stated in the entirety of the *Ṣaṣṭitantra*.
However, [the sūtra states]: "They are devoid of narratives (ākhyāyikā), free from the doctrines of others, and pure.
Here, *ākhyāyikā* means a narrative (*ākhyāna*); they are devoid of such.

Because it is free from the objections raised by others, it is pure and absolute; since it has demonstrated the objects that are most useful for bondage and liberation, this *Saptati* is therefore complete. // 72 //
Thus ends the Commentary on the Sāṃkhyasaptati composed by Śrī Śaṅkarabhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the worshipful Śrī Govinda Bhagavatpāda.
